pagetitle: "Gauge symmetry and the Kaluza-Klein tower"

# Gauge symmetry and the Kaluza-Klein tower {#sec-kk-gauge-tower}

The reduction of the previous chapter produced a vector field $A_\mu$ whose action is Maxwell's. For it to be the
electromagnetic potential it must also have Maxwell's symmetry, the abelian gauge invariance $A_\mu \to A_\mu -
\partial_\mu\epsilon$ of @sec-gauge-theories, and charged matter must couple to it with quantised charges. Both properties
come from the circle. A coordinate change that shifts the position on each circle by an amount depending on the
spacetime point leaves the form of the ansatz intact and acts on $A_\mu$ as a gauge transformation: gauge invariance is
a part of five-dimensional general covariance, and the gauge group is the isometry group $U(1)$ of the circle. Once
fields are allowed to depend on the circle coordinate, each of them becomes an infinite tower of four-dimensional
fields, the Kaluza-Klein modes, whose masses and charges are both proportional to the momentum around the circle, so
that charge is quantised because momentum on a circle is.

The chapter has two sections. The first derives the gauge transformation from the reparametrisations of the circle,
as a matrix identity, and identifies the gauge symmetry with the Killing vector $\partial_y$ of
@sec-flows-killing. The second expands fields in the Fourier series of @sec-fourier-series, finds the masses $|n|/R$
and the charges $ne$ of the tower from the spectrum of $-\partial_y^2$, a self-adjoint operator in the sense of
@sec-unbounded-operators, proves that periodicity forces integer charges, and relates the radius of the circle to the
Planck length and the fine-structure constant. The numbers show both the success and the problem of the
five-dimensional theory: charge is quantised and the gauge coupling is predicted, but the charged states are as heavy
as the Planck mass. The same Fourier analysis describes a field at finite temperature (@sec-thermal-circle), and the
tower is the simplest example of an ultraviolet completion of a four-dimensional effective theory
(@sec-renormalisation). A third section, @sec-kk-fermions, expands a five-dimensional fermion in the same way and
finds its magnetic moment, its spin structures and why the circle gives no chiral fermions. Every statement is followed by
three examples and three exercises with hidden solutions.

## Gauge invariance from the fifth dimension {#sec-kk-gauge}

The vector field of the ansatz is a gauge field: a coordinate change along the circle, $y \mapsto y + \epsilon(x)$,
leaves the ansatz in its form and shifts $A_\mu$ by the gradient of $\epsilon$. This section derives that
transformation, identifies the five-dimensional origin of the $U(1)$ gauge symmetry of @sec-abelian-gauge, and
relates it to the Killing vector $\partial_y$, following @overduin1998 [Sec. 4.3] and @duff1994 [Sec. 2].

### Reparametrising the circle

The ansatz singles out the circle coordinate $y$, but nothing in five-dimensional geometry fixes where $y = 0$ is on
each circle. Choosing the origin independently over each spacetime point is a coordinate change, and it is the one
that does not disturb the cylinder condition.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-circle-reparametrisation}
#### Reparametrisation of the circle

A **reparametrisation of the circle** is the five-dimensional coordinate change
$$
x'^\mu = x^\mu, \qquad y' = y + \epsilon(x),
$$ {#eq-circle-shift}
with $\epsilon$ a function on spacetime: the same point of $M_4 \times S^1$ is labelled by a circle coordinate shifted
by an amount depending on where one is in spacetime. Its Jacobian $\partial x^A/\partial x'^B$ is the identity on
spacetime, $\partial y/\partial x'^\mu = -\partial_\mu\epsilon$, $\partial y/\partial y' = 1$ (@def-kk-jacobian).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The two-dimensional toy shows the effect of the shift on a picture. The first example is the computation behind
@fig-kk-gauge-shift.

::: {#exm-shift-cylinder}
#### On the cylinder

For the two-dimensional ansatz the lines of constant $y'$ wind relative to those of constant $y$ (left panel of
@fig-kk-gauge-shift); in the chart $(x, y')$ the Riemannian toy $dx^2 + \phi^2(dy + A\,dx)^2$ is $dx^2 + \phi^2(dy' + (A -
\epsilon')dx)^2$ (the sign of the circle block plays no role).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Checked with SageManifolds in `figures/kk_gauge_shift.sage`.
:::

A shift by the same amount everywhere is a rigid rotation of every circle. The second example identifies it with
the isometry of the circle and with a global symmetry.

::: {#exm-shift-constant}
#### A constant shift

$\epsilon = c$ rotates the circle rigidly and changes nothing: it is the $U(1)$ isometry generated by $\partial_y$
(@def-isometry-u1), and the gauge transformation with constant parameter is a global symmetry
(@def-global-local-symmetry).
:::

The new coordinate must again be a coordinate on a circle. The third example checks the periodicity and points to the
subtlety of large gauge transformations.

::: {#exm-shift-periodicity}
#### Periodicity

$\epsilon(x)$ need not be periodic in anything, but $y'$ must again be a circle coordinate: $y' \sim y' + 2\pi$ holds
automatically since $y \sim y + 2\pi$ and $\epsilon$ is single valued. The large gauge transformations with $\epsilon$
winding are the subtlety behind $\mathbb{R}$ versus $U(1)$ in @exm-isometry-r-vs-u1.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![The gauge transformation as a coordinate change along the circle. Left: lines of constant $y$ (gray) and of
constant $y' = y + \epsilon(x)$ (red) on the cylinder, for $\epsilon = 0.8\sin x$. Right: the gauge field in the two

Generated by `figures/kk_gauge_shift.sage`.](figures/kk_gauge_shift.svg){#fig-kk-gauge-shift width=90%}

Reparametrisations can be composed. The first exercise shows that they form an abelian group, the group of gauge
transformations. The answer identifies the gauge group.

::: {#exr-kkr-shift-composition}
#### Composing shifts

Show that the shift by $\epsilon_1$ followed by the shift by $\epsilon_2$ is the shift by $\epsilon_1 + \epsilon_2$, that the inverse
of the shift by $\epsilon$ is the shift by $-\epsilon$, and that the transformations commute. Which group is this when $\epsilon$
takes values in $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$y'' = y' + \epsilon_2(x) = y + \epsilon_1(x) + \epsilon_2(x)$, and $x$ is untouched, so the composition is the shift by $\epsilon_1 +
\epsilon_2$, the identity is $\epsilon = 0$ and the inverse is $-\epsilon$; addition of functions is commutative. With $y \sim y +
2\pi$ the shift by $\epsilon$ and by $\epsilon + 2\pi$ act identically, so the group is that of maps from spacetime to
$U(1) = \mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}$ with pointwise multiplication: the abelian gauge group of @def-gauge-field-u1.
:::

In two dimensions the shift can remove the gauge field altogether. The second exercise does so with SageManifolds and
explains why this is impossible in five dimensions.

::: {#exr-kkr-shift-remove-a}
#### Removing $A$ in two dimensions

For the toy $dx^2 + \phi(x)^2(dy + A(x)dx)^2$ choose $\epsilon$ with $\epsilon' = A$ and verify with SageManifolds that the metric
becomes $dx^2 + \phi^2dy'^2$. Why can one not do the same with $A_\mu(x)$ in four dimensions?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\epsilon = \int A\,dx$, $A' = A - \epsilon' = 0$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-shift-remove-a >}}

In four dimensions $A' = A - d\epsilon = 0$ requires $A = d\epsilon$, so $F = dA = 0$: a gauge field with non-zero field
strength cannot be removed, and the field strength is exactly what survives in the reduced action
(@exm-gauge-f-invariant). In one spacetime dimension every one-form is exact, which is why the toy has no field
strength (@exr-kk-toy).
:::

The horizontal curves of @fig-kk-circle are drawn without reference to coordinates. The third exercise shows that they
are unchanged by a reparametrisation, although $A$ changes.

::: {#exr-kkr-shift-horizontal}
#### Horizontal curves are invariant

A curve $(x(s), y(s))$ is horizontal if $\dot y + A_\mu\dot x^\mu = 0$, i.e. if its tangent is orthogonal to $\partial_y$. Show
that a curve horizontal for $(y, A)$ is horizontal for $(y', A')$, and interpret the winding of the horizontal curves
around a closed loop in spacetime.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\dot y' + A'_\mu\dot x^\mu = \dot y + \partial_\mu\epsilon\,\dot x^\mu + (A_\mu - \partial_\mu\epsilon)\dot x^\mu = \dot y + A_\mu\dot x^\mu$: the condition
is the same, as it must be since orthogonality to $\partial_y$ is geometric (@exr-kkr-horizontal-lift). Following a
horizontal curve around a closed loop $\gamma$ in spacetime shifts $y$ by $-\oint_\gamma A = -\int_\Sigma F$ for a surface $\Sigma$
bounded by $\gamma$: the holonomy, gauge invariant because $F$ is; it is the Aharonov-Bohm phase of a particle of
unit momentum around the circle.
:::
::::

### The gauge transformation

The reparametrisation acts on the metric through its Jacobian. Because only the circle coordinate changes, the
Jacobian has a simple triangular form, and the transformation of the ansatz becomes a product of three block
matrices.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-kk-jacobian}
#### Jacobian of the shift

The **Jacobian** of @eq-circle-shift is the $5 \times 5$ matrix $J = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -\partial\epsilon^T & 1
\end{pmatrix}$ in the blocks $(x^\mu, y)$, with $\det J = 1$; a metric transforms as $\hat g' = J^T\hat gJ$
(@def-tensor-field).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The inverse Jacobian belongs to the inverse shift. The first example writes it and reads off the group law. Both follow from the triangular form of the matrix.

::: {#exm-jacobian-inverse}
#### Its inverse

$J^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \partial\epsilon^T & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, the Jacobian of the inverse shift $y = y' -
\epsilon$: two shifts compose by adding their $\epsilon$, the group law of $U(1)$ gauge transformations.
:::

A unit determinant means that volumes are preserved. The second example draws the consequence for the volume
element of the ansatz.

::: {#exm-jacobian-volume}
#### Volume preserved

$\det J = 1$, so $\sqrt{|\hat g|}$ is unchanged, consistent with @eq-kk-volume: $\phi$ and $g$ do not transform.
:::

The shifts are only part of the five-dimensional diffeomorphisms. The third example places them among all those that
preserve the cylinder condition.

::: {#exm-jacobian-general}
#### General five-dimensional diffeomorphisms

A general $\xi^A(x, y)$ mixes the Fourier modes of @sec-kk-tower; the transformations preserving the cylinder
condition have $\xi^\mu = \xi^\mu(x)$, $\xi^y = \epsilon(x)$, and generate the four-dimensional diffeomorphisms of
@def-kk-fields together with the gauge transformations [@duff1994, eqs. 9-10].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the group law of @exm-jacobian-inverse at the level of matrices. It is a computation with
symbolic gradients.

::: {#exr-kkr-jacobian-compose}
#### The group of Jacobians

Verify with Sage that $J(\epsilon_1)J(\epsilon_2) = J(\epsilon_1 + \epsilon_2)$, $J(\epsilon)^{-1} = J(-\epsilon)$, $\det J = 1$ and that the
Jacobians commute.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The gradients $\partial\epsilon_1$, $\partial\epsilon_2$ are independent symbols:

{{< sage exr-kkr-jacobian-compose >}}

The map $\partial\epsilon \mapsto J(\epsilon)$ is a homomorphism from the additive group of gradients into the unipotent lower
triangular matrices.
:::

The Jacobian of @def-kk-jacobian is $\partial x/\partial x'$. The second exercise computes $\partial x'/\partial x$ directly and checks
that it is the inverse.

::: {#exr-kkr-jacobian-direction}
#### Which Jacobian?

Compute the matrix $\partial x'^A/\partial x^B$ of @eq-circle-shift and show that it is $J^{-1}$. Why does the metric transform
with $J = \partial x/\partial x'$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial x'^\mu/\partial x^\nu = \delta^\mu_\nu$, $\partial x'^\mu/\partial y = 0$, $\partial y'/\partial x^\nu = \partial_\nu\epsilon$, $\partial y'/\partial y = 1$:
$\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ \partial\epsilon^T & 1 \end{pmatrix} = J^{-1}$ (@exm-jacobian-inverse). The metric components are
covariant, $\hat g'_{AB} = \frac{\partial x^C}{\partial x'^A}\frac{\partial x^D}{\partial x'^B}\hat g_{CD}$ (@def-tensor-field), so they
transform with $\partial x/\partial x' = J$; contravariant objects such as $\hat g^{AB}$ transform with $J^{-1}$
(@exr-kkr-gauge-inverse-metric).
:::

Gauge transformations and four-dimensional coordinate changes can be combined. The third exercise writes the
Jacobian of the combination and its action on the fields.

::: {#exr-kkr-jacobian-general}
#### The combined transformation

For $x'^\mu = x'^\mu(x)$, $y' = y + \epsilon(x)$, write the Jacobian $\partial x/\partial x'$ in blocks and the transformation of
$(g, A, \phi)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $L^\nu{}_\mu = \partial x^\nu/\partial x'^\mu$: $\partial y/\partial x'^\mu = -L^\nu{}_\mu\partial_\nu\epsilon$, so $\partial x/\partial x' =
\begin{pmatrix} L & 0 \\ -\partial\epsilon^TL & 1 \end{pmatrix} = J(\epsilon)\operatorname{diag}(L, 1)$. The metric transforms first by the
shift and then by the four-dimensional change: $g' = L^TgL$, $A' = L^T(A - \partial\epsilon)$, $\phi' = \phi$, combining
@exr-kk-tensor-law and @eq-kk-gauge.
:::
::::

The Jacobian acting on the ansatz gives back the ansatz with a shifted vector. This is the central fact of the
section, the five-dimensional origin of gauge invariance.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-kk-gauge-transformation}
#### The Kaluza-Klein gauge transformation

Under @eq-circle-shift the ansatz keeps its form with
$$
g'_{\mu\nu} = g_{\mu\nu}, \qquad \phi' = \phi, \qquad A'_\mu = A_\mu - \partial_\mu\epsilon ,
$$ {#eq-kk-gauge}
since $dy + A\,dx = dy' + (A - d\epsilon)dx$ [@overduin1998, eq. 30; @duff1994, eq. 10]: the coordinate freedom along
the circle is the abelian gauge transformation of @def-gauge-field-u1 (@prp-kk-gauge-shift). The four-dimensional
theory inherits a $U(1)$ gauge invariance from five-dimensional general covariance.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A gauge transformation must leave the field strength invariant. The first example checks this and concludes that the
reduced action is gauge invariant.

::: {#exm-gauge-f-invariant}
#### $F$ is invariant

$F'_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu(A_\nu - \partial_\nu\epsilon) - \partial_\nu(A_\mu - \partial_\mu\epsilon) = F_{\mu\nu}$ by the symmetry of second
derivatives, the content of @prp-covariant-u1; so the reduced action @eq-kk-reduced-action is gauge invariant, as
it must be, being a coordinate-invariant five-dimensional action evaluated on a form-invariant ansatz.
:::

The transformation is a matrix identity. The second example writes the block products that prove it. Each block reduces to a short polynomial identity.

::: {#exm-gauge-matrix}
#### As a matrix identity

$J^T\hat g(g, A, \phi)J = \hat g(g, A - \partial\epsilon, \phi)$ for the block matrix of @exm-ansatz-matrix: the
$(\mu\nu)$ block gives $g - \phi^2AA^T + \phi^2(A\,\partial\epsilon^T + \partial\epsilon\,A^T) - \phi^2\partial\epsilon\,\partial\epsilon^T = g -
\phi^2(A - \partial\epsilon)(A - \partial\epsilon)^T$, the mixed block $-\phi^2(A - \partial\epsilon)$, the corner $-\phi^2$
(@prp-kk-gauge-shift, @exr-kk-gauge-shift).
:::

Fields that depend on $y$ transform too. The third example shows that they acquire phases, the transformation of
charged fields.

::: {#exm-gauge-charged-modes}
#### Charged modes

A mode $f_n(x)e^{iny/R}$ of a five-dimensional field becomes $f_n(x)e^{in(y' - \epsilon)/R}$: the four-dimensional
field $f_n$ acquires the phase $e^{-in\epsilon/R}$, the gauge transformation of a field of charge $n/R$
(@def-covariant-derivative-u1); the charge is the momentum around the circle (@sec-kk-tower).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the gauge invariance of the reduced action term by term. It uses the invariance of the
abelian field strength under a gauge transformation.

::: {#exr-kk-f-invariant}
#### Gauge invariance of the reduced action

Show that each term of @eq-kk-reduced-action is invariant under @eq-kk-gauge.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g$ and $\phi$ are unchanged, so $\sqrt{-g}$, $R$ and the prefactor $\phi$ are; $F_{\mu\nu}$ is invariant by
@exm-gauge-f-invariant, so $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ is. @prp-covariant-u1 is exactly the statement needed, with $\alpha = -\epsilon$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.FieldTheory.abelian_F_invariant` (@prp-covariant-u1), with $\alpha = -\epsilon$.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The inverse metric must transform consistently with the metric. The second exercise checks that it does, with the same
shift of $A$.

::: {#exr-kkr-gauge-inverse-metric}
#### The inverse ansatz

Verify with Sage that $J^{-1}\hat g^{-1}(A)J^{-T} = \hat g^{-1}(A - \partial\epsilon)$ for the inverse ansatz @eq-kk-inverse, with
$g^{\mu\nu}$ as free symbols.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Inverting $\hat g' = J^T\hat gJ$ gives $\hat g'^{-1} = J^{-1}\hat g^{-1}J^{-T}$, and the claim is that the right-hand side is
again of the form @eq-kk-inverse:

{{< sage exr-kkr-gauge-inverse-metric >}}

Only $\hat g^{\mu y} = -A^\mu$ and $\hat g^{yy}$ change; $\hat g^{\mu\nu} = g^{\mu\nu}$ is gauge invariant.
:::

The frame one-form $e^y = dy + A_\mu dx^\mu$ is the natural object on the five-dimensional space. The third exercise shows
that it does not depend on the choice of circle coordinate.

::: {#exr-kkr-gauge-frame}
#### The connection one-form

Show that $e^y = dy + A_\mu dx^\mu$ equals $dy' + A'_\mu dx^\mu$, and that $de^y = \tfrac12F_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu \wedge dx^\nu$. Why does this
make $A$ a connection on the circle bundle?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$dy' + A'_\mu dx^\mu = dy + \partial_\mu\epsilon\,dx^\mu + (A_\mu - \partial_\mu\epsilon)dx^\mu = dy + A_\mu dx^\mu$: $e^y$ is a well-defined
one-form on $M_4 \times S^1$, while $A$ depends on the coordinate $y$. Its exterior derivative is $d(A_\mu dx^\mu) =
\partial_\nu A_\mu\,dx^\nu \wedge dx^\mu = \tfrac12F_{\nu\mu}dx^\nu \wedge dx^\mu$, the curvature. A one-form on the total space that
is invariant under the circle action and equal to $dy$ on the fibres is a connection, and $A$ is its local
expression: the Kaluza-Klein gauge field is a connection on the circle bundle in the sense of
@def-bundle-connection, and $F$ is its curvature (@def-curvature-connection).
:::
::::

### The isometry

The gauge symmetry is generated by a vector field on the five-dimensional space, the generator of rotations of the
circle. Its defining property is that it preserves the metric, which is the cylinder condition in invariant form.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-isometry-u1}
#### The circle isometry

The vector field $\partial_y$ is a Killing vector of every metric satisfying the cylinder condition
(@def-killing), and its flow $y \mapsto y + c$ is a one-parameter group of isometries; since $y$ is
periodic the group is $U(1)$, and its orbits are the circles of constant $x$. The gauge group of the reduced theory
is the isometry group of the internal space, here $U(1)$ for $S^1$; for a general internal space it is the group
of its Killing vectors (Part IV).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In adapted coordinates the Killing equation is trivial. The first example checks it. No computation is needed beyond the definition of the Lie derivative.

::: {#exm-isometry-killing}
#### Killing's equation

$\mathcal{L}_{\partial_y}\hat g_{AB} = \partial_y\hat g_{AB} = 0$ by @def-cylinder-condition (the Lie derivative along a
coordinate vector field is the partial derivative, @def-lie-derivative): the Killing equation holds identically.
:::

The group generated by $\partial_y$ is $U(1)$ only because $y$ is periodic. The second example explains when the
periodicity is visible.

::: {#exm-isometry-r-vs-u1}
#### $\mathbb{R}$ versus $U(1)$

The zero-mode theory alone has no memory of the periodicity of $y$: its gauge group is $\mathbb{R}$, and the
compactness of $U(1)$, with the quantisation of charge, appears only when the massive modes are kept [@duff1994,
p. 6] (@def-charge-quantisation).
:::

Every continuous symmetry has a conserved charge. The third example identifies the charge of the circle isometry. It is the bridge to the Kaluza-Klein tower of the next section.

::: {#exm-isometry-charge}
#### Charge as momentum

The Noether charge of the $U(1)$ isometry is the momentum $p_y$ along the circle, $-i\partial_y = n/R$ on the mode
$e^{iny/R}$: the electric charge of a Kaluza-Klein particle is its momentum in the fifth dimension, and charge
conservation is momentum conservation along $y$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise shows that the infinitesimal gauge transformation is the Lie derivative along $\epsilon(x)\partial_y$. It
connects the gauge transformation with the flows of @sec-flows-killing.

::: {#exr-kk-lie-derivative}
#### The Killing vector

Compute the Lie derivative of the ansatz metric along $\xi = \epsilon(x)\partial_y$ and show that it reproduces
$\delta A_\mu = -\partial_\mu\epsilon$ infinitesimally.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g_{AB} = \xi^C\partial_C\hat g_{AB} + \partial_A\xi^C\hat g_{CB} + \partial_B\xi^C\hat g_{AC}$ (@eq-lie-metric) with
$\xi^y = \epsilon$, $\xi^\mu = 0$: the first term vanishes by the cylinder condition, and $\partial_\mu\xi^y = \partial_\mu\epsilon$
gives $\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g_{\mu\nu} = -\partial_\mu\epsilon\,\phi^2A_\nu - \partial_\nu\epsilon\,\phi^2A_\mu$, $\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g_{\mu y} = -
\partial_\mu\epsilon\,\phi^2$, $\mathcal{L}_\xi\hat g_{yy} = 0$. Comparing with the variation of @eq-kk-components under
$\delta A_\mu$: $\delta\hat g_{\mu y} = -\phi^2\delta A_\mu$, so $\delta A_\mu = \partial_\mu\epsilon$ for the active transformation,
that is $-\partial_\mu\epsilon$ for the passive coordinate change @eq-kk-gauge, with $\delta g = \delta\phi = 0$.
:::

The second exercise repeats @exr-kk-lie-derivative with SageManifolds in three dimensions. It also shows that
$\epsilon(x)\partial_y$ is not a Killing vector unless $\epsilon$ is constant.

::: {#exr-kkr-isometry-killing}
#### Killing vectors with SageManifolds

For the ansatz in $2 + 1$ dimensions with arbitrary functions, compute $\mathcal{L}_{\partial_y}\hat g$ and $\mathcal{L}_{\epsilon\partial_y}\hat
g$, and compare the latter with $\frac{d}{ds}\hat g(A + s\,d\epsilon)|_{s = 0}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-kkr-isometry-killing >}}

$\mathcal{L}_{\epsilon\partial_y}\hat g_{ty} = -\phi^2\partial_t\epsilon$ vanishes only for constant $\epsilon$: the local transformations are not
isometries; they are symmetries of the reduced theory because they act on the fields, not because they preserve a
given metric.
:::

The Killing vector field has a dual one-form, obtained by lowering its index. The third exercise shows that it contains
the gauge field.

::: {#exr-kkr-isometry-one-form}
#### The Killing one-form

Lower the index of $K = \partial_y$ with @eq-kk-components. Show that $K_A dx^A = -\phi^2e^y$, that $\hat g(K, K) = -\phi^2$,
and recover $A_\mu$ and $\phi$ from $K$ and $\hat g$ alone.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$K_A = \hat g_{Ay}$: $K_\mu = -\phi^2A_\mu$ and $K_y = -\phi^2$, so $K_Adx^A = -\phi^2(dy + A_\mu dx^\mu) = -\phi^2e^y$ and $\hat
g(K, K) = K_y = -\phi^2$. Hence $\phi^2 = -\hat g(K, K)$ and $A_\mu = K_\mu/K_y$: the Kaluza-Klein fields are geometric
data of the pair (metric, Killing vector), the size of the orbits and the one-form orthogonal to them, which is how
the reduction generalises to other isometry groups (Part IV).
:::
::::

The proposition of this section is the matrix identity behind the gauge transformation. It holds for any
$4 \times 4$ block, not only for metrics.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-kk-gauge-shift}
#### The gauge shift

$J^T\hat gJ = \hat g'$ with $\hat g$ the ansatz for $(g, A, \phi)$, $\hat g'$ the ansatz for $(g, A - \partial\epsilon, \phi)$
and $J$ the Jacobian of @def-kk-jacobian, for any $4 \times 4$ matrix $g$, vectors $A$, $\partial\epsilon$ and scalar
$\phi$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Gauge.gauge_shift >}}

**Sage.** Checked with SageManifolds in five dimensions in @exr-kk-gauge-shift.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A constant shift has the identity as Jacobian. The first example records this trivial case of the proposition. It shows which transformations act on the zero modes.

::: {#exm-kkr-gauge-constant}
#### A constant shift

For constant $\epsilon$, $\partial\epsilon = 0$, $J = 1$ and the identity is $\hat g = \hat g$: the rigid rotations of
@exm-shift-constant act trivially on the zero modes, and only on the modes with $n \neq 0$ (@exm-gauge-charged-modes).
:::

A linear shift changes a constant potential by a constant. The second example shows that a constant $A$ is pure gauge.

::: {#exm-kkr-gauge-linear}
#### A constant potential is pure gauge

For $\epsilon = c_\mu x^\mu$, $\partial\epsilon = c$ is constant and the proposition gives $A' = A - c$: a constant potential can be
shifted to zero. In the five-dimensional picture, $\hat g(g, c, \phi)$ is the flat metric in the sheared coordinates
$(x, y - c_\mu x^\mu)$, which is why a constant $A$ has no physical effect, apart from a holonomy around closed loops
when spacetime itself has non-contractible circles.
:::

The proposition does not assume that $g$ is a metric. The third example comments on its form. Its generality makes the proof a pure computation.

::: {#exm-kkr-gauge-any-matrix}
#### The generality of the statement

The identity holds for any matrix $g$ and any $A$, $\partial\epsilon$ and $\phi$, with $\partial\epsilon$ an arbitrary vector rather
than a gradient: the integrability of $\partial\epsilon$ plays no role at a point. Splitting the indices into the four
spacetime ones and the circle one, the matrix products expand block by block, and each entry is a polynomial
identity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Gauge.gauge_shift` splits the indices into the blocks of $\text{Fin}\,4 \oplus \text{Unit}$,
expands the matrix products and closes each entry with `ring`.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise is the five-dimensional check of the proposition with SageManifolds. It uses a genuine change of
chart rather than matrices.

::: {#exr-kk-gauge-shift}
#### The shifted chart in SageManifolds

Write the five-dimensional ansatz in the chart $(x, y + \epsilon(x))$ and read off the transformed fields.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-kk-gauge-shift >}}
:::

The finite transformation of the proposition and the infinitesimal one of @exr-kk-lie-derivative must agree. The
second exercise expands the first to first order.

::: {#exr-kkr-gauge-infinitesimal}
#### The infinitesimal form

Replace $\epsilon$ by $s\epsilon$ in @prp-kk-gauge-shift and expand to first order in $s$. Compare with the Lie derivative of
@exr-kk-lie-derivative.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\hat g(A - s\,\partial\epsilon) = \hat g(A) - s\frac{\partial\hat g}{\partial A}\cdot\partial\epsilon + O(s^2)$, with the first-order term
$\phi^2(A_\mu\partial_\nu\epsilon + A_\nu\partial_\mu\epsilon)$ in the $(\mu\nu)$ block and $\phi^2\partial_\mu\epsilon$ in the mixed block: minus the Lie
derivative $\mathcal{L}_{\epsilon\partial_y}\hat g$ of @exr-kk-lie-derivative. The sign is the difference between the passive
coordinate change (components in the new chart) and the active transformation (the metric pulled back along the
flow).
:::

A gauge field of the form $A = d\chi$ is pure gauge. The third exercise interprets this in five dimensions.

::: {#exr-kkr-gauge-pure-gauge}
#### Pure gauge

Show that the ansatz with $A = d\chi$ for a function $\chi$ is the ansatz with $A = 0$ in the coordinate $y + \chi$. What
does this imply for the Ricci tensor of the first metric?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\epsilon = \chi$, @eq-kk-gauge gives $A' = d\chi - d\chi = 0$, so in the chart $(x, y + \chi)$ the metric is $g -
\phi^2dy'^2$. The two are the same metric in two charts, so all curvature invariants agree, and the frame components of
the Ricci tensor of @exr-kkr-ricci-frame are those of the $A = 0$ metric: $F = 0$ removes every Maxwell term from
@eq-kk-ricci.
:::
::::

## The Kaluza-Klein tower {#sec-kk-tower}

Klein's contribution was to take the fifth dimension seriously as a circle: every field is a Fourier series in
$y$, each mode is a four-dimensional particle with a mass and a charge fixed by its momentum around the circle, and
the quantisation of electric charge follows from periodicity. This section defines the mode expansion, the masses
and charges of the tower, the zero-mode truncation and the relation between the radius, the Planck mass and the
gauge coupling, following @duff1994 [Sec. 2] and @overduin1998 [Secs. 4.1-4.2]. Here the circle coordinate has period $2\pi R$ and the scalar is set to $\phi = 1$ in the ground state, which
is the same geometry as $y \sim y + 2\pi$ with $\phi = R$ (@exr-kkr-volume-circle).

### Fourier modes

A function on a circle is determined by its Fourier coefficients (@sec-fourier-series). Applied to the circle
coordinate of a five-dimensional field, the expansion turns one field into infinitely many four-dimensional ones,
labelled by an integer.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-fourier-modes}
#### Fourier modes on the circle

A field on $M_4 \times S^1$ with $y \sim y + 2\pi R$ has the expansion
$$
\Phi(x, y) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}\phi_n(x)\,e^{iny/R}, \qquad \phi_{-n} = \phi_n^*\ \text{for real}\ \Phi,
$$ {#eq-fourier-modes}
the **Kaluza-Klein modes**; the same expansion applies to each component of the metric [@duff1994, eqs. 5-6].
The mode $e^{iny/R}$ is an eigenfunction of $\partial_y^2$ with eigenvalue $-(n/R)^2$ (@prp-kk-modes), and the
modes are orthogonal, $\int_0^{2\pi R}e^{i(n - m)y/R}dy = 2\pi R\,\delta_{nm}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest field to expand is a massless scalar. The first example derives the equations of its modes. The equation obtained is the one stated in @prp-kk-modes.

::: {#exm-modes-scalar}
#### A massless scalar

For $\Box_5\Phi = 0$ with $\Box_5 = \hat g^{AB}\partial_A\partial_B = \Box_4 - \partial_y^2$ in the signature $(+, -, -, -, -)$,
inserting @eq-fourier-modes gives $(\Box_4 + (n/R)^2)\phi_n = 0$ mode by mode (@exr-kk-modes), the Klein-Gordon
equation of @sec-conventions-indices with $m^2 = (n/R)^2$: an infinite set of four-dimensional Klein-Gordon fields
with masses $|n|/R$.
:::

The metric itself has modes. The second example lists them and anticipates their reorganisation into massive
spin-two fields. The counting is completed in the next subsection.

::: {#exm-modes-metric}
#### The metric modes

$g_{\mu\nu}(x, y) = \sum_ng_{\mu\nu,n}(x)e^{iny/R}$ and likewise $A_\mu$, $\phi$: the $n = 0$ modes are the Kaluza-Klein fields
of @def-kk-fields, the $n \neq 0$ modes of $g_{\mu\nu}$ are massive spin-$2$ fields, and the $n \neq 0$ modes of $A_\mu$
and $\phi$ are eaten by them [@duff1994, p. 7] (@exr-kk-spin2).
:::

The symmetries have modes too. The third example describes the algebra they generate. It is much larger than the symmetry of the zero modes.

::: {#exm-modes-gauge-parameters}
#### The gauge parameters

The diffeomorphism parameters $\hat\xi^A(x, y)$ expand too; their $n \neq 0$ modes generate an infinite-dimensional
algebra of Kac-Moody-Virasoro type that contains the Poincaré and $U(1)$ algebras of the zero modes [@duff1994,
eq. 15].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![The Kaluza-Klein tower. Left: the masses $|n|/R$ of the modes $e^{iny/R}$ for two radii, each level carrying
the charge $ne$. Right: the real parts of the first three mode functions around the circle. The eigenvalue
$(n/R)^2$ of $-\partial_y^2$ and the periodicity condition are checked symbolically. Generated by
`figures/kk_tower.sage`; in the interactive version a slider sets $R$ and the title counts the modes lighter than
$E = 2$.](figures/kk_tower.svg){#fig-kk-tower width=90%}

{{< interactive kk_tower 460 >}}

A real field has complex modes. The first exercise works out the constraint that reality imposes on them. The answer pairs each mode with its antiparticle.

::: {#exr-kkr-modes-reality}
#### Real fields

Show that $\Phi$ is real if and only if $\phi_{-n} = \phi_n^*$ for all $n$, and rewrite the expansion of a real field as a
sum of cosines and sines. How many real four-dimensional fields are there at each mass level $n \neq 0$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Phi^* = \sum_n\phi_n^*e^{-iny/R} = \sum_n\phi_{-n}^*e^{iny/R}$, and uniqueness of Fourier coefficients gives $\Phi^* = \Phi$ iff
$\phi_{-n}^* = \phi_n$. Then $\Phi = \phi_0 + \sum_{n \geq 1}(2\operatorname{Re}\phi_n\cos(ny/R) - 2\operatorname{Im}\phi_n\sin(ny/R))$, with $\phi_0$
real. Each level $n \geq 1$ carries two real fields, $\operatorname{Re}\phi_n$ and $\operatorname{Im}\phi_n$, equivalently one complex
field: a charged particle and its antiparticle (@exm-charge-conjugation).
:::

A field profile around the circle determines which modes are present. The second exercise computes the modes of a
square wave with Sage.

::: {#exr-kkr-modes-square-wave}
#### The modes of a square wave

Find the Kaluza-Klein modes of the profile $\Phi(y) = 1$ for $0 < y < \pi R$, $-1$ for $\pi R < y < 2\pi R$, and check
Parseval's identity $\frac{1}{2\pi R}\int_0^{2\pi R}|\Phi|^2dy = \sum_n|\phi_n|^2$. Which masses does the profile contain?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\phi_n = \frac{1}{2\pi R}\int_0^{2\pi R}\Phi e^{-iny/R}dy = \frac{2}{i\pi n}$ for odd $n$ and $0$ for even $n$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-modes-square-wave >}}

The profile has no zero mode and contains only the odd levels, masses $|n|/R$ with $n$ odd, with weights falling like
$1/n$: a sharp profile around the circle is built from arbitrarily heavy modes.
:::

The orthogonality of the modes makes the action diagonal. The third exercise shows that the five-dimensional action of
a scalar becomes a sum of four-dimensional actions, one per mode.

::: {#exr-kkr-modes-action}
#### The action mode by mode

For a complex massless scalar with action $\int d^4x\int_0^{2\pi R}dy\,\hat g^{AB}\partial_A\Phi^*\partial_B\Phi$ on flat $M_4 \times S^1$,
insert @eq-fourier-modes and integrate over $y$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\hat g^{AB}\partial_A\Phi^*\partial_B\Phi = \partial_\mu\Phi^*\partial^\mu\Phi - |\partial_y\Phi|^2$. With the modes, $\int dy\,\partial_\mu\Phi^*\partial^\mu\Phi = 2\pi
R\sum_n\partial_\mu\phi_n^*\partial^\mu\phi_n$ and $\int dy\,|\partial_y\Phi|^2 = 2\pi R\sum_n(n/R)^2|\phi_n|^2$, the cross terms vanishing by
orthogonality. The action is $2\pi R\sum_n\int d^4x(\partial_\mu\phi_n^*\partial^\mu\phi_n - (n/R)^2|\phi_n|^2)$: decoupled complex
Klein-Gordon fields of masses $|n|/R$, each with the normalisation factor $2\pi R$ that is absorbed into the
fields.
:::
::::

### Masses and charges

The mode number $n$ appears twice in the four-dimensional physics: in the mass, through the eigenvalue of $-\partial_y^2$,
and in the charge, through the phase that a gauge transformation produces. Both are fixed by the radius.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-kk-mass}
#### Kaluza-Klein mass

The **mass** of the mode $n$ is $m_n = |n|/R$: the five-dimensional massless wave equation on
$\phi_n(x)e^{iny/R}$ is the four-dimensional one with $m_n^2 = (n/R)^2$ (@prp-kk-modes, @exr-kk-modes), and the
masses grow without bound, an infinite **tower** (@fig-kk-tower).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
If the circle is as small as the Planck length, the masses are huge. The first example puts in the numbers.

::: {#exm-mass-planck}
#### Planck-scale masses

If $R$ is of the order of the Planck length, $m_1 \sim 10^{19}\,\text{GeV}$: the first massive mode is twenty-two
orders of magnitude heavier than the electron, the discrepancy that "played a large role in the abandonment of
five-dimensional Kaluza-Klein theory" [@overduin1998, p. 23] (@exr-kk-numbers).
:::

The massive modes of the metric combine into massive spin-two particles. The second example counts their degrees of
freedom. The count is the one of @exr-kk-spin2.

::: {#exm-mass-spin2}
#### Massive spin two

The mode $g_{\mu\nu,n}$ has $5$ degrees of freedom, obtained by eating the $2$ of $A_{\mu,n}$ and the $1$ of $\phi_n$
in addition to its own $2$: the massive spectrum is pure spin $2$ [@duff1994, p. 7] (@exr-kk-spin2).
:::

The masses depend on the size of the circle, which is the dynamical scalar. The third example states the dependence
in the two frames of @sec-kk-einstein-frame.

::: {#exm-mass-radius}
#### Varying $\phi$

With a non-constant $\phi$ the mode $n$ has the mass $|n|/(R\phi)$ measured with the Jordan metric, the inverse local
radius $R\phi$ of the circle (@exm-charge-covariant-derivative), and $|n|/(R\phi^{3/2})$ in the Einstein frame
(@exr-kkr-mass-einstein-frame, @fig-kkr-couplings): the tower's spacing is set by the local size of the circle,
which is why $\phi$ must be stabilised.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise counts the polarisations of the massive modes of the metric. It is the gravitational analogue of
the Higgs mechanism.

::: {#exr-kk-spin2}
#### Degrees of freedom of a massive mode

Count the degrees of freedom of the modes $g_{\mu\nu,n}$, $A_{\mu,n}$, $\phi_n$ for $n \neq 0$ and show they match a
massive spin-$2$ field.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A massless graviton has $2$ polarisations, a massless vector $2$, a scalar $1$: $5$ in all, the number of
polarisations of a massive spin-$2$ particle ($2s + 1$ with $s = 2$). The $n \neq 0$ gauge parameters $\xi^\mu_n$,
$\xi^y_n$ can be used to set $A_{\mu,n}$ and $\phi_n$ to zero, after which $g_{\mu\nu,n}$ is a massive spin-$2$ field
with $5$ polarisations [@duff1994, p. 7]: a gravitational Higgs mechanism, the analogue of @def-higgs-mechanism
with the vector and the scalar as the eaten modes.
:::

The dependence of the mass on $\phi$ in @exm-mass-radius can be derived from the wave equation. The second exercise
does so with SageManifolds for constant $\phi$.

::: {#exr-kkr-mass-einstein-frame}
#### The mass in the Einstein frame

For constant $\phi$ write the ansatz with the Einstein-frame metric $g^E = \eta$, i.e. $\phi^{-1}\eta - \phi^2dy^2$, and solve
$\Box_5\Phi = 0$ on $\Phi = f(t)e^{iny/R}$. Deduce the masses in both frames.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
SageManifolds gives $\Box_5\Phi\,e^{-iny/R} = \phi(f'' + \frac{n^2}{R^2\phi^3}f)$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-mass-einstein-frame >}}

So $m_E = |n|/(R\phi^{3/2})$ with respect to $g^E = \eta$. The Jordan metric $\phi^{-1}\eta$ has proper time $t_J = t/\sqrt\phi$,
and $m_J^2 = \phi m_E^2 = n^2/(R\phi)^2$, in agreement with @exr-kkr-einstein-masses.
:::

A five-dimensional field may itself be massive. The third exercise shows how the tower shifts. The result is used again for the thermal circle.

::: {#exr-kkr-mass-massive}
#### A massive five-dimensional field

Find the four-dimensional masses of the modes of a five-dimensional scalar with $(\Box_5 + M^2)\Phi = 0$. What is the
lightest mass, and how many modes have mass below $2M$ when $MR = 3$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On a mode, $\Box_5 = \Box_4 + (n/R)^2$, so $(\Box_4 + M^2 + n^2/R^2)\phi_n = 0$ and $m_n^2 = M^2 + n^2/R^2$: the masses add in
quadrature, the lightest is $M$ (the zero mode). Below $2M$: $M^2 + n^2/R^2 < 4M^2$ iff $|n| < \sqrt3MR = 3\sqrt3 \approx 5.2$,
so $n = -5, \dots, 5$: eleven modes.
:::
::::

The charge of a mode is read off from its gauge transformation. Since the phase of the mode $n$ is proportional to
$n$, all charges are integer multiples of one unit, which is fixed by the gravitational coupling and the radius.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-charge-quantisation}
#### Charge quantisation

Under the gauge transformation @eq-kk-gauge the mode $\phi_n$ transforms by $e^{-in\epsilon/R}$ (@exm-gauge-charged-modes), so
it has charge $q_n = n/R$ in the units of @eq-kk-ansatz, or $q_n = ne$ with $e = \sqrt2\kappa/R$ once the Maxwell
term is canonically normalised [@duff1994, eq. 16]. Periodicity of $e^{iny/R}$ under $y \to y + 2\pi R$ forces
$n \in \mathbb{Z}$ (@prp-kk-periodicity): electric charge is quantised in units of $e$, Klein's explanation of
charge quantisation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The charge can also be read off from the coupling to the gauge field in the action. The first example expands the
five-dimensional kinetic term and finds the covariant derivative.

::: {#exm-charge-covariant-derivative}
#### From the covariant derivative

$\hat g^{AB}\partial_A\Phi\,\partial_B\Phi^*$ with @eq-kk-inverse contains $-A^\mu(\partial_\mu\Phi\,\partial_y\Phi^* + \partial_y\Phi\,\partial_\mu\Phi^*) +
(A_\mu A^\mu - \phi^{-2})|\partial_y\Phi|^2$, which on the mode $n$ assembles into $g^{\mu\nu}(\partial_\mu - inA_\mu/R)\phi_n
(\partial_\nu + inA_\nu/R)\phi_n^*$ minus the mass term $\phi^{-2}(n/R)^2|\phi_n|^2$ [@overduin1998, eq. 24]: the covariant derivative @eq-covariant-derivative-u1 with charge $n/R$.
:::

The integrality of $n$ is the whole content of charge quantisation. The second example shows what fails for a
non-integer $n$.

::: {#exm-charge-integer}
#### Why integers

$e^{in(y + 2\pi R)/R} = e^{iny/R}e^{2\pi in}$, and $e^{2\pi in} = 1$ exactly when $n \in \mathbb{Z}$: for $n = \tfrac12$ the mode
changes sign around the circle (@fig-kk-tower). The general statement rests on $\exp z = \exp w \iff z - w \in 2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$ (@prp-kk-periodicity).
:::

Opposite charges correspond to opposite momenta. The third example identifies charge conjugation with a reflection
of the circle. It explains the reality condition of @def-fourier-modes.

::: {#exm-charge-conjugation}
#### Charge conjugation

$n \to -n$ is the reflection $y \to -y$ of the circle: charge conjugation is parity in the fifth dimension
[@duff1994, p. 8], and the reality condition $\phi_{-n} = \phi_n^*$ pairs particles with antiparticles.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise verifies @exm-charge-covariant-derivative with Sage. The derivatives of the mode are treated as
independent symbols, as in the jet computations of @sec-kk-reduction.

::: {#exr-kkr-charge-covariant}
#### The covariant derivative in Sage

For $\Phi = f(x)e^{iny/R}$ and the inverse ansatz with $g^{\mu\nu}$ free, verify that $\hat g^{AB}\partial_A\Phi\,\partial_B\Phi^* =
g^{\mu\nu}D_\mu f\,(D_\nu f)^* - \phi^{-2}(n/R)^2|f|^2$ with $D_\mu = \partial_\mu - inA_\mu/R$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-kkr-charge-covariant >}}

The identity is exact: no term of the five-dimensional kinetic term is lost, and the minimal coupling with charge $n/R$
is forced by the geometry.
:::

A field may return to itself up to a phase after going around the circle. The second exercise shows how such twisted
boundary conditions shift the charges.

::: {#exr-kkr-charge-twisted}
#### Twisted boundary conditions

Suppose $\Phi(x, y + 2\pi R) = e^{2\pi i\theta}\Phi(x, y)$ with $0 < \theta < 1$. Find the allowed modes, their masses and their
charges. Is there a massless mode?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{iky/R}$ satisfies the condition when $e^{2\pi ik} = e^{2\pi i\theta}$, i.e. $k = n + \theta$ with $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. The masses are
$|n + \theta|/R$ and the charges $(n + \theta)/R$: still evenly spaced, but shifted, and no mode is massless. For $\theta = \tfrac12$
(antiperiodic fields, as fermions at finite temperature, @exr-kkr-truncation-thermal) the charges are half-integers;
charge quantisation in the strict sense, all charges being integer multiples of one unit, requires that every field
be periodic.
:::

All modes of the tower have the same charge-to-mass ratio. The third exercise compares it with that of the electron.

::: {#exr-kkr-charge-ratio}
#### Charge to mass

Compute $q_n/m_n$ for $n \neq 0$ with $q_n = ne$, $m_n = |n|/R$ and $e = \sqrt2\kappa/R$. Compare with the electron, for which
$e/m_e \approx 7 \times 10^{21}\sqrt{G}$ in units $\hbar = c = 1$, and conclude whether the electron can be a Kaluza-Klein
mode.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$q_n/m_n = \pm ne/(|n|/R) = \pm\sqrt2\kappa = \pm4\sqrt{\pi G}$, independent of $n$ and of $R$: every mode has a charge-to-mass ratio
of gravitational size, the extremality bound of @exm-radius-black-holes. The electron's ratio is about $10^{21}$
times larger, so it cannot be a mode of the tower: its mass would have to be $10^{21}$ times smaller than $1/R$, i.e.
the electron would have to be a zero mode with a mass from some other source, while the zero modes are neutral.
:::
::::

### The zero modes and the radius

At energies far below $1/R$ only the zero modes can be excited. The theory then reduces to the four-dimensional theory
of @sec-kk-reduction, and the only trace of the circle is the relation between the couplings and the radius.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-zero-mode-truncation}
#### Zero-mode truncation

The **zero-mode truncation** keeps only the $n = 0$ modes of every field: it is the cylinder condition
(@def-cylinder-condition), it is consistent because zero modes never source non-zero ones, and it yields the
reduced theory of @sec-kk-reduction. Truncating instead to finitely many massive modes is inconsistent
[@duff1994, p. 8].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The truncation is justified physically by the mass gap. The first example states it. It is an energy argument, valid only below $1/R$.

::: {#exm-truncation-light}
#### The light sector

For $R$ small all $n \neq 0$ modes are heavier than any energy available: the zero modes are the whole observable
theory, with $U(1)$ gauge invariance and a massless scalar. The massive modes are the signature of the extra
dimension, visible only at energies $\sim 1/R$.
:::

Consistency is a separate requirement from lightness. The second example defines it and notes where it fails. The circle is the case in which it holds exactly.

::: {#exm-truncation-consistency}
#### Consistency

A truncation is consistent when every solution of the truncated equations lifts to a solution of the full ones;
for the circle this holds because products of $y$-independent fields are $y$-independent. For spheres (Part IV) it
fails for the naive ansatz, the consistency problem of @overduin1998 [Sec. 4.4].
:::

The truncated theory forgets the periodicity. The third example draws the consequence for the gauge group. The global structure of the group is invisible to the zero modes.

::: {#exm-truncation-gauge-group}
#### $\mathbb{R}$ not $U(1)$

The truncated theory has lost the periodicity of $y$: its gauge group is $\mathbb{R}$ (@exm-isometry-r-vs-u1), and
the charge quantisation of @def-charge-quantisation is visible only in the full tower.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Interactions between modes conserve the momentum around the circle. The first exercise shows this for a cubic
interaction with Sage, and draws the consequence for the truncation.

::: {#exr-kkr-truncation-cubic}
#### A cubic interaction

For the interaction $\lambda\int dy\,\Phi^3$ of a five-dimensional scalar, show that the modes $n_1, n_2, n_3$ couple with
strength proportional to $\int_0^{2\pi R}e^{i(n_1 + n_2 + n_3)y/R}dy$, and evaluate it.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Inserting @eq-fourier-modes, $\int dy\,\Phi^3 = \sum_{n_1, n_2, n_3}\phi_{n_1}\phi_{n_2}\phi_{n_3}\int dy\,e^{i(n_1 + n_2 + n_3)y/R}$ and the
integral is $2\pi R\,\delta_{n_1 + n_2 + n_3, 0}$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-truncation-cubic >}}

Momentum (charge) is conserved at each vertex. Two zero modes can only produce a zero mode, so setting the massive
modes to zero is consistent; two massive modes $n$ and $-n$ produce a zero mode, so the converse truncation is not.
:::

Keeping a few massive modes is tempting but wrong. The second exercise shows why with the same selection rule. The selection rule leaves no intermediate option.

::: {#exr-kkr-truncation-finite}
#### Finite truncations

Show that a truncation of $\Phi$ to the modes $n = 0, \pm1$ is inconsistent for the cubic interaction of
@exr-kkr-truncation-cubic. Which modes must be added, and where does the process stop?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The vertex $(1, 1, -2)$ is allowed, so the equation of $\phi_{-2}$ (equivalently $\phi_2^*$) is sourced by $\phi_1^2$: setting
$\phi_{\pm2} = 0$ contradicts its field equation whenever $\phi_1 \neq 0$. Adding $\pm2$ brings in $\pm3$, $\pm4$ and so on:
the process never stops, and the only consistent truncations are to the zero modes or to the full tower. This is the
precise sense of the statement in @def-zero-mode-truncation.
:::

A field at temperature $T$ lives on a Euclidean time circle of circumference $1/T$. The third exercise applies the
Kaluza-Klein reasoning to it.

::: {#exr-kkr-truncation-thermal}
#### The thermal circle

In the Euclidean formulation of @sec-thermal-circle, bosonic fields are periodic in imaginary time with period $\beta =
1/T$ and fermionic fields antiperiodic. Using the Matsubara frequencies of @def-matsubara-frequency, find the
"Kaluza-Klein masses" of the three-dimensional modes and explain why a high-temperature field theory is effectively
three-dimensional.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Periodic fields have modes $e^{2\pi in\tau/\beta}$, frequencies $\omega_n = 2\pi nT$, so a massless boson gives three-dimensional
fields of masses $2\pi|n|T$; antiperiodic fermions have $\omega_n = (2n + 1)\pi T$, masses at least $\pi T$, and no zero mode
(@exr-kkr-charge-twisted with $\theta = \tfrac12$). At high temperature all non-zero modes are heavy compared with the
other scales, and the long-distance physics is that of the bosonic zero modes in three dimensions: dimensional
reduction, with the circle of circumference $1/T$ shrinking as $T$ grows.
:::
::::

The gauge coupling of the reduced theory is not a free parameter: it is fixed by the gravitational coupling and the
radius. Inverting this relation determines the size of the circle from the measured charge.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-planck-radius-relation}
#### Radius-coupling relation

With $2\pi\kappa^2R = \hat\kappa^2$ (@exr-frame-newton) and $e = \sqrt2\kappa/R$, the three parameters of the theory, the
five-dimensional Newton constant, the radius and the electric charge unit, are related by
$$
R = \frac{\sqrt2\,\kappa}{e}, \qquad \kappa^2 = 8\pi G_4 = \frac{8\pi}{M_P^2} ,
$$ {#eq-radius-coupling}
so that for $e$ the electron charge $R$ is of order the Planck length [@duff1994, p. 8] (@prp-kk-radius).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The relation can be evaluated with the measured fine-structure constant. The first example does so. The result is a radius of about two dozen Planck lengths.

::: {#exm-radius-numbers}
#### The numbers

$e^2/4\pi = \alpha \approx 1/137$ and $\kappa = \sqrt{8\pi}/M_P$ give $R = \sqrt2\kappa/e = \sqrt{4/\alpha}\,/M_P \approx 23/M_P
\sim 4 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{m}$: a circle about two dozen Planck lengths in radius (@exr-kk-numbers).
:::

The relation can be read the other way. The second example predicts the fine-structure constant from the radius. This is the form in which @overduin1998 states it.

::: {#exm-radius-fine-structure}
#### The fine-structure constant

Conversely, $\alpha = 4/(M_P^2R^2\phi)$ in the conventions of @overduin1998 [eq. 26]: a Planck-size circle predicts
$\alpha$ of order one, so the smallness of $\alpha$ requires $R$ somewhat larger than the Planck length, and the
masses of the tower are then slightly below the Planck mass.
:::

The massive modes have a remarkable charge-to-mass ratio. The third example connects them with black holes. The coincidence is no accident (Part VI).

::: {#exm-radius-black-holes}
#### Extreme black holes

The charge-to-mass ratio $e_n/m_n = \sqrt2\kappa$ of the modes is exactly the extremality bound of the charged
Kaluza-Klein black holes [@duff1994, eq. 19]: the massive Kaluza-Klein states are extreme black holes, a hint
of the dualities of Part VI.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise estimates the radius and the first mass from the measured couplings. It is the computation behind
@exm-radius-numbers.

::: {#exr-kk-numbers}
#### The size of the circle

Using $\alpha = e^2/4\pi \approx 1/137$ and $M_P \approx 1.2 \times 10^{19}\,\text{GeV}$, estimate $R$ and $m_1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e = \sqrt{4\pi\alpha} \approx 0.30$ and $\kappa = \sqrt{8\pi}/M_P$, so $R = \sqrt2\kappa/e = \sqrt{16\pi}/(eM_P) \approx 7.1/(0.30\,M_P)
\approx 23/M_P \approx 2 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{GeV}^{-1} \approx 4 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{m}$, and $m_1 = 1/R \approx 5 \times
10^{17}\,\text{GeV}$: the first charged mode is a few percent of the Planck mass, and no mode is light. Different
conventions for $\kappa$ and $e$ shift these by factors of order one (@overduin1998 finds $\alpha \sim 4$ for
$R = \ell_P$ exactly).
:::

Modern models consider much larger extra dimensions. The second exercise shows that a TeV-size circle is incompatible
with the Kaluza-Klein photon being the photon.

::: {#exr-kkr-radius-tev}
#### A TeV circle

Suppose $m_1 = 1/R = 1\,\text{TeV}$. Compute with Sage the gauge coupling $e = \sqrt2\kappa/R$ and $\alpha = e^2/4\pi$. What
does this imply for models with TeV-size extra dimensions?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\alpha = 4/(M_PR)^2$ with $M_PR = 1.22 \times 10^{16}$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-radius-tev >}}

$\alpha \approx 3 \times 10^{-32}$: the Kaluza-Klein gauge field of a TeV circle is far too weakly coupled to be the photon.
Models with large or TeV-size extra dimensions therefore put the Standard Model gauge fields elsewhere (on a brane, or
in a different sector), and use the circle only for gravity (@arkanihamed1998).
:::

The relation involves couplings of different dimensions. The third exercise checks the dimensions, a useful habit in
a theory with several Newton constants.

::: {#exr-kkr-radius-dimensions}
#### Dimensions

In units $\hbar = c = 1$, find the dimensions of $\hat\kappa^2$, $\kappa^2$, $e$ and $R$, and check $2\pi R\kappa^2 = \hat\kappa^2$ and
$R = \sqrt2\kappa/e$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The action is dimensionless, $\int d^Dx\sqrt{|g|}R$ has dimension $\text{length}^{D - 2}$, so $\kappa_D^2$ has dimension
$\text{length}^{D - 2}$: $\hat\kappa^2 \sim \text{length}^3$ and $\kappa^2 \sim \text{length}^2$. The charge $e$ is dimensionless in four
dimensions ($\alpha = e^2/4\pi$). Then $2\pi R\kappa^2 \sim \text{length}^3$ matches $\hat\kappa^2$, and $\sqrt2\kappa/e \sim \text{length}$
matches $R$.
:::
::::

The tower and its relation to the radius rest on four identities. The first is the eigenvalue equation of the modes and
the four-dimensional wave equation it implies.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-kk-modes}
#### The mode functions

$\partial_y^2e^{iny/R} = -(n/R)^2e^{iny/R}$, and on a product mode the five-dimensional Klein-Gordon operator
$\Box_5 = \Box_4 - \partial_y^2$ gives the four-dimensional one with mass squared $(n/R)^2$, $(\Box_4 + (n/R)^2)\phi_n$.
:::

`mass_of_mode` for $m_n = |n|/R$.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Tower.deriv2_mode >}}

**Sage.** Checked symbolically in `figures/kk_tower.sage` and @exr-kk-modes.

::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The zero mode is the massless one. The first example records it, with the fields it describes. These are the fields of the reduced theory of the previous chapter.

::: {#exm-kkr-modes-zero}
#### The zero mode

For $n = 0$ the mode function is constant, $\partial_y^2 1 = 0$, and $\phi_0$ obeys $\Box_4\phi_0 = 0$: the massless field of the
zero-mode truncation. For the metric these are the graviton, the photon and the dilaton of @def-kk-fields.
:::

The first massive level is doubly degenerate. The second example evaluates it. The degeneracy is a consequence of the reflection symmetry of the circle.

::: {#exm-kkr-modes-first-level}
#### The first level

For $R = 1$ the modes $n = \pm1$ have $m^2 = 1$, $e^{\pm iy}$ being the two eigenfunctions of $-\partial_y^2$ with eigenvalue $1$, or
equivalently $\cos y$ and $\sin y$. Every level $n \neq 0$ is doubly degenerate, as the slider of @fig-kk-tower shows by
the symmetric pattern of masses.
:::

The mass formula is the four-dimensional reading of the five-dimensional dispersion relation. The third example makes
this explicit. It is the particle picture of the wave equation.

::: {#exm-kkr-modes-dispersion}
#### A massless particle in five dimensions

A plane wave $e^{-i(Et - \vec p\cdot\vec x - p_yy)}$ with $p_y = n/R$ solves $\Box_5\Phi = 0$ when $E^2 = \vec p^2 + p_y^2$: a massless
five-dimensional particle, null with respect to $\hat g$. Four-dimensional observers see $E^2 = \vec p^2 + m_n^2$ with $m_n = |
p_y|$: mass is momentum in the hidden direction.
:::
::::

The first exercise expands a five-dimensional massless scalar in modes with Sage. It also derives the
four-dimensional Klein-Gordon equation of each mode.

::: {#exr-kk-modes}
#### The tower of a massless scalar

Expand a five-dimensional massless scalar in modes and derive the four-dimensional equations, orthogonality and
periodicity with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-kk-modes >}}

:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Tower.klein_gordon_mode >}}

**Sage.** The solution above (@exr-kk-modes).
:::

An interval instead of a circle gives a different tower. The second exercise computes it with Sage, for Dirichlet and
Neumann conditions.

::: {#exr-kkr-modes-interval}
#### Modes on an interval

On $0 \leq y \leq \pi R$ find the eigenfunctions of $-\partial_y^2$ with Dirichlet conditions $\Phi = 0$ and with Neumann conditions
$\partial_y\Phi = 0$ at both ends. Compare the spectra with that of the circle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Dirichlet: $\sin(ny/R)$, $n \geq 1$; Neumann: $\cos(ny/R)$, $n \geq 0$; eigenvalues $(n/R)^2$ in both cases:

{{< sage exr-kkr-modes-interval >}}

The masses are those of the circle, but each level appears once instead of twice, and the Dirichlet tower has no zero
mode. The interval is the circle divided by the reflection $y \to -y$, and the two boundary conditions keep the
odd and the even functions; such orbifolds remove unwanted massless fields.
:::

The eigenfunctions of $-\partial_y^2$ form a complete orthogonal system. The third exercise places this in the theory of
unbounded operators.

::: {#exr-kkr-modes-self-adjoint}
#### The circle Laplacian

Consider $-\partial_y^2$ on $L^2(S^1)$ with domain the periodic functions with square-integrable second derivative. Using
@sec-unbounded-operators and @sec-fourier-series, explain why it is self-adjoint, find its spectrum, and why every field
on the circle is a superposition of Kaluza-Klein modes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the Fourier basis $e_n = e^{iny/R}/\sqrt{2\pi R}$, which is orthonormal and complete in $L^2(S^1)$, the operator is
multiplication by $(n/R)^2$: its domain is the set of $\sum c_ne_n$ with $\sum n^4|c_n|^2 < \infty$, on which it is symmetric,
and a multiplication operator by a real sequence on its maximal domain is self-adjoint. The spectrum is $\{n^2/R^2 : n
\in \mathbb{Z}\}$, purely discrete with multiplicity $2$ for $n \neq 0$; completeness of the eigenvectors is the
completeness of the Fourier series, which is why the expansion @eq-fourier-modes loses nothing.
:::
::::

The second identity is the periodicity condition. It is the mathematical core of charge quantisation. Its proof uses only the periodicity of the exponential function.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-kk-periodicity}
#### Charge quantisation

$e^{in(y + 2\pi R)/R} = e^{iny/R}$ if and only if $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, for $R \neq 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.**

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Tower.periodic_iff_int >}}

**Sage.** @exr-kkr-periodicity-check.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A half-integer mode is the simplest failure of periodicity. The first example describes it and where it nonetheless
appears. Such modes appear when fields are allowed to change sign around the circle.

::: {#exm-kkr-periodicity-half}
#### $n = \tfrac12$

$e^{i(y + 2\pi R)/2R} = -e^{iy/2R}$: the mode changes sign around the circle. It is not a function on the circle, but it is a
section of the twisted (Möbius) line bundle over it, and fermions with antiperiodic boundary conditions, as at
finite temperature, are expanded in such modes (@exr-kkr-charge-twisted).
:::

Rational values of $n$ are periodic after several turns. The second example counts them. They live on a larger circle.

::: {#exm-kkr-periodicity-rational}
#### Rational $n$

For $n = p/q$ in lowest terms, $e^{in(y + 2\pi kR)/R} = e^{iny/R}e^{2\pi ikp/q}$ is periodic after $k = q$ turns and not before: such
a mode lives on the $q$-fold cover of the circle, a circle of radius $qR$, on which it is the integer mode $p$.
:::

Irrational values are never periodic. The third example notes the consequence for a field theory on the circle. They live on no circle at all.

::: {#exm-kkr-periodicity-irrational}
#### Irrational $n$

For $n = \sqrt2$ the phases $e^{2\pi i\sqrt2k}$, $k = 1, 2, \dots$, never return to $1$ and are dense on the unit circle: the
mode is not a function on any finite cover. A field theory on the circle has only integer modes, and the charges of
all its states are commensurate.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the periodicity criterion with Sage on integers, rationals and an irrational. It mirrors
the three examples.

::: {#exr-kkr-periodicity-check}
#### Periodicity in Sage

Evaluate $e^{2\pi iq}$ for $q = 0, 1, -2, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \tfrac25$, find after how many turns $q = \tfrac25$ returns, and check
numerically that $q = \sqrt2$ does not return within fifty turns.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-kkr-periodicity-check >}}
:::

The proof of the proposition uses one property of the exponential. The second exercise reconstructs the argument from that property alone.

::: {#exr-kkr-periodicity-proof}
#### The proof

Prove @prp-kk-periodicity from the fact that $e^z = 1$ if and only if $z \in 2\pi i\mathbb{Z}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{in(y + 2\pi R)/R} = e^{iny/R}$ iff $e^{2\pi in} = 1$, dividing by the non-zero $e^{iny/R}$, iff $2\pi in = 2\pi ik$ for some $k \in
\mathbb{Z}$, iff $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. The radius cancels, which is why the hypothesis $R \neq 0$ is only needed to make $y/R$
meaningful.
:::

Periodicity also restricts the gauge parameters. The third exercise shows that this makes the gauge group compact. The argument shows that charge quantisation and compactness are equivalent.

::: {#exr-kkr-periodicity-gauge-group}
#### The gauge group is compact

Show that the gauge transformations with parameters $\epsilon$ and $\epsilon + 2\pi R$ act identically on every mode $\phi_n$ with $n
\in \mathbb{Z}$, so that the gauge group is $U(1) = \mathbb{R}/2\pi R\mathbb{Z}$. What would change if a mode with $n = \tfrac12$ were
present?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\phi_n \mapsto e^{-in\epsilon/R}\phi_n$ and $e^{-in(\epsilon + 2\pi R)/R} = e^{-in\epsilon/R}e^{-2\pi in} = e^{-in\epsilon/R}$ for integer $n$: the shift by
$2\pi R$ acts trivially and the group is $\mathbb{R}/2\pi R\mathbb{Z} \cong U(1)$. A mode with $n = \tfrac12$ changes sign under
the shift by $2\pi R$, so only $4\pi R$ would act trivially: the group would be a double cover, still $U(1)$ but with
the unit of charge halved. Compactness of the gauge group and quantisation of charge are the same statement
(@exm-isometry-r-vs-u1).
:::
::::

The last identity inverts the normalisation of the charge. Its content is algebraic; the normalisation itself is
taken from the literature.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-kk-radius}
#### The radius from the coupling

$e = \sqrt2\kappa/R$ gives $R = \sqrt2\kappa/e$; the normalisation $e = \sqrt2\kappa/R$ itself is taken from @duff1994 [eq.
16].
:::

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Tower.radius_of_coupling` (an algebraic identity); the normalisation is cited, not derived.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The radius is expressed most usefully through $\alpha$ and $M_P$. The first example rewrites the proposition in these
terms. It is the form used in numerical estimates.

::: {#exm-kkr-radius-alpha}
#### In terms of $\alpha$

With $\kappa = \sqrt{8\pi}/M_P$ and $e = \sqrt{4\pi\alpha}$: $R = \sqrt2\sqrt{8\pi}/(M_P\sqrt{4\pi\alpha}) = 2/(\sqrt\alpha\,M_P)$. The radius is
inversely proportional to the square root of the fine-structure constant: a weaker electromagnetism needs a larger
circle.
:::

The normalisation was derived in @exr-kkr-action-normalisation. The second example retraces the steps that lead
to it. The factor $\sqrt2$ is a consequence of the normalisation of the Einstein-Hilbert action.

::: {#exm-kkr-radius-origin}
#### Where $\sqrt2\kappa/R$ comes from

The reduced action has $-\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\cdot\tfrac14F^2$ with $A$ the potential of the coordinate $y$ of period $2\pi R$
(dimensionless $A$); the canonical field is $\mathcal{A} = A/(\sqrt2\kappa)$, and the mode $n$ couples through $\partial - i(n/R)A =
\partial - in(\sqrt2\kappa/R)\mathcal{A}$ (@exm-charge-covariant-derivative). So the unit of charge is $\sqrt2\kappa/R$.
:::

The proposition fixes one of the three parameters in terms of the others. The third example lists what is predicted
and what is input.

::: {#exm-kkr-radius-parameters}
#### Inputs and predictions

The five-dimensional theory has two parameters, $\hat\kappa$ and $R$. Four-dimensional physics measures $\kappa$ (Newton's
constant) and $e$ (the electron charge, if it were a Kaluza-Klein charge): $R = \sqrt2\kappa/e$ and $\hat\kappa^2 = 2\pi R\kappa^2$
follow, and the masses $|n|/R$ of the tower are then a prediction, the unsuccessful one of @exm-mass-planck.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise solves the relation with Sage and evaluates it. It checks the closed form of @exm-kkr-radius-alpha. The numerical value is the one quoted in @exm-radius-numbers.

::: {#exr-kkr-radius-solve}
#### Solving for the radius

Solve $e = \sqrt2\kappa/R$ for $R$ with Sage, substitute $\kappa^2 = 8\pi/M_P^2$ and $e^2 = 4\pi\alpha$, and evaluate $RM_P$ for $\alpha =
1/137.036$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-kkr-radius-solve >}}

$R \approx 23.4/M_P$, in agreement with @exr-kk-numbers.
:::

The relation can be written with the five-dimensional coupling. The second exercise eliminates $\kappa$. The result explains the exponent in @fig-kkr-couplings.

::: {#exr-kkr-radius-five-dimensional}
#### In five-dimensional terms

Using $\hat\kappa^2 = 2\pi R\kappa^2$, express $e^2$ through $\hat\kappa$ and $R$. How does the charge unit scale with the radius at
fixed five-dimensional coupling?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^2 = 2\kappa^2/R^2 = 2\hat\kappa^2/(2\pi R \cdot R^2) = \hat\kappa^2/(\pi R^3)$. At fixed $\hat\kappa$ the charge unit falls like $R^{-3/2}$:
a larger circle dilutes both gravity ($\kappa^2 \propto 1/R$) and electromagnetism, the latter faster. This is the
$\phi^{-3/2}$ of @fig-kkr-couplings, with $R\phi$ the radius.
:::

Above the energy $1/R$ the four-dimensional theory is replaced by the five-dimensional one. The third exercise relates
this to the effective field theories of @sec-renormalisation.

::: {#exr-kkr-radius-effective-theory}
#### The tower as an ultraviolet completion

Count the modes with mass below a cutoff $\Lambda$, and estimate how a one-loop sum over the tower of a quantity that
receives a contribution $c$ from each mode below $\Lambda$ grows with $\Lambda$. In the sense of @def-effective-field-theory, what
is the cutoff of the four-dimensional zero-mode theory, and what replaces it above?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The modes with $|n|/R < \Lambda$ number $2\lfloor\Lambda R\rfloor + 1 \approx 2\Lambda R$ (the count of the interactive @fig-kk-tower), so
such a sum grows like $2c\Lambda R$, one power of $\Lambda$ more than a single field would give: above $1/R$ the theory
behaves as a five-dimensional one, with five-dimensional power counting. The zero-mode theory is an effective
field theory valid below $\Lambda \sim 1/R$, where the first massive modes appear; above it the tower, i.e. the
five-dimensional theory, takes over, itself an effective theory below its own Planck scale $\hat\kappa^{-2/3}$.
:::
::::

## Fermions on the circle {#sec-kk-fermions}

The two previous sections expanded bosonic fields on the circle. A five-dimensional fermion gives a tower too, but with
three new features. Its covariant derivative contains the spin connection of the ansatz, which couples the spin of every
mode to the field strength $F_{\mu\nu}$ and changes the magnetic moment; it may be periodic or antiperiodic around the
circle, the two spin structures of @exm-spd-spin-circle, which shifts the masses and halves the unit of charge; and its
four-dimensional modes always come in left-right pairs, so the circle cannot produce the chiral fermions of the Standard
Model, while the orbifold $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$ can. The algebra of five-dimensional spinors, the spectrum of $i\,d/dy$ for
every twist and the orbifold projection are in @sec-spinors-dirac-operator (@exr-spd-five-four, @def-scherk-schwarz-twist,
@exm-spd-s1z2); this section does the physics, following @perezlorenzana2005 [Secs. III.A, IV.C-D and V.1] for the
towers and the orbifold and @duff1998gyromagnetic [Sec. 2] for the magnetic moment. Throughout, $\phi = 1$ and $y \sim y + 2\pi
R$, as in @sec-kk-tower.

### The Dirac operator on $M^4 \times S^1$

On the Kaluza-Klein ansatz the five-dimensional Dirac operator splits into the four-dimensional operator with the
covariant derivative of charge $n/R$, the internal operator whose eigenvalues are the masses, and one more term, built from
the spin connection, that couples the spin to $F_{\mu\nu}$. The figure shows its effect on the Landau levels of the first
massive mode.

![The lowest Landau levels of the first massive Kaluza-Klein fermion in a weak magnetic field (solid), compared with an
elementary Dirac particle of the same charge and mass (dashed), in the non-relativistic limit $E - m = \omega(N + \tfrac12) -
\tfrac12 g\omega s$ with $\omega = |q|B/m$ and $s = \pm\tfrac12$. The Kaluza-Klein mode has $g = 1$ (@prp-kkf-mode-equation), so
its spin splitting is half as large and its lowest level rises as $\tfrac14\omega$; for $g = 2$ the lowest level stays at $E =
m$. The spin-connection term and the chiral rotation that produce $g = 1$ are checked with explicit gamma matrices.
Generated by `figures/kkf-zeeman.sage`; the interactive version adds the level $N = 2$.](figures/kkf-zeeman.svg){#fig-kkf-zeeman width=70%}

{{< interactive kkf-zeeman 460 >}}

The definition needs a frame for the ansatz. The natural one makes the fifth leg the one-form $dy + A$ that already
appears in the line element, so that the gauge field enters the frame rather than the gamma matrices.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-kkf-five-dirac}
#### Five-dimensional Dirac operator

On $M^4 \times S^1$ with the ansatz $d\hat s^2 = g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - (dy + A_\mu dx^\mu)^2$ of @def-kk-ansatz at $\phi
= 1$, take the frame and its dual
$$
\hat E^a = e^a{}_\mu dx^\mu, \quad \hat E^4 = dy + A_\mu dx^\mu, \qquad \hat E_a = e_a{}^\mu(\partial_\mu - A_\mu\partial_y), \quad
\hat E_4 = \partial_y ,
$$ {#eq-kkf-frame}
with $\eta_{AB} = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1, -1)$, and the gamma matrices $\Gamma^a = \gamma^a$, $\Gamma^4 = i\gamma_5$ of
@exr-spd-five-four. The torsion-free spin connection, $d\hat E^A + \omega^A{}_B \wedge \hat E^B = 0$, is
$$
\omega_{ab} = \mathring\omega_{ab} + \tfrac12F_{ab}\hat E^4, \qquad \omega_{4a} = -\tfrac12F_{ab}\hat E^b ,
$$ {#eq-kkf-spin-connection}
with $\mathring\omega$ that of $e^a$ and $F_{ab} = e_a{}^\mu e_b{}^\nu F_{\mu\nu}$. The **five-dimensional Dirac operator** is
$i\Gamma^A\hat E_A{}^M\nabla_M$ with $\nabla_M = \partial_M + \tfrac14\omega_{AB M}\Gamma^A\Gamma^B$, and on the ansatz it reads
$$
i\Gamma^A\nabla_A = i\gamma^ae_a{}^\mu(\mathring\nabla_\mu - A_\mu\partial_y) - \gamma_5\partial_y - \tfrac{i}{8}F_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b\,i\gamma_5 ,
$$ {#eq-kkf-dirac}
where $\mathring\nabla$ is the spinor covariant derivative of $g_{\mu\nu}$. The last term, the **Pauli term**, comes from the
mixed components $\omega_{4a}$ and $\omega_{ab}(\hat E_4)$ of the spin connection. For $A = 0$ and $g = \eta$ the operator is the
flat one of @perezlorenzana2005 [eqs. (35)-(38)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
When the gauge field vanishes the frame is a product, the Pauli term drops out and the operator is that of a flat
five-dimensional space. The first example records this case, which @sec-spinors-dirac-operator treats in full.

::: {#exm-kkf-flat-five}
#### The product $M^4 \times S^1$

For $A = 0$ and $g = \eta$, @eq-kkf-dirac is $i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - \gamma_5\partial_y$: on $\psi = \chi(x)e^{iny/R}$ it becomes
$(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - i\tfrac nR\gamma_5)\chi$, the equation of @exr-spd-branch-mass with $\lambda = -n/R$, and the
four-dimensional mass is $|n|/R$. A five-dimensional Dirac spinor has four complex components, a four-dimensional Dirac spinor
at every level [@perezlorenzana2005, eqs. (35)-(36)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A constant gauge field has no field strength, so it changes only the derivative. The second example shows that it is
removed by the reparametrisation of @def-circle-reparametrisation, exactly as for scalars.

::: {#exm-kkf-constant-a}
#### A constant potential

For constant $A_\mu$ and $g = \eta$ the operator is $i\gamma^\mu(\partial_\mu - A_\mu\partial_y) - \gamma_5\partial_y$; on the mode $n$ the
first term is $i\gamma^\mu(\partial_\mu - i\tfrac nRA_\mu)$. The shift $y \to y + A_\mu x^\mu$ maps the frame @eq-kkf-frame to
that of $A = 0$ and multiplies the mode by $e^{-inA_\mu x^\mu/R}$ (@exm-gauge-charged-modes): a pure gauge, as long as no spatial
direction is compact (@exr-kkr-int-charged-scalar).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Only $F_{\mu\nu}$ can appear besides the minimal coupling, because the operator is covariant under the gauge
transformations of @def-kk-gauge-transformation. The third example identifies the term it produces.

::: {#exm-kkf-field-strength}
#### The coupling to the field strength

With $\Gamma^4 = i\gamma_5$ the Pauli term is $\tfrac18F_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma_5$, a matrix that commutes with $\gamma_5$ and
anticommutes with every $\gamma^\mu$: it has the chirality structure of a mass term, and after the chiral rotation of
@exr-spd-branch-mass it becomes the magnetic dipole coupling $-\tfrac18\sigma^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}$ with $\sigma^{\mu\nu} =
\tfrac{i}{2}[\gamma^\mu, \gamma^\nu]$ (@exr-kkf-gamma-contraction). Its coefficient is fixed by the geometry and does not depend on the
mode number.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
