:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The spin connection @eq-kkf-spin-connection was guessed and checked. The first exercise checks it with Sage, as a
statement about differential forms.

::: {#exr-kkf-cartan}
#### The structure equations

Take $e^a = dx^a$ on flat $\mathbb{R}^4$ and an arbitrary potential $A_\mu(x)$. Verify with Sage that @eq-kkf-spin-connection
satisfies $d\hat E^A + \omega^A{}_B \wedge \hat E^B = 0$ for $A = 0, \dots, 4$ and that $\omega_{AB} = -\omega_{BA}$, by writing all
two-forms in the basis $\hat E^A \wedge \hat E^B$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\hat E^4 = dy + A$, $d\hat E^4 = dA = \tfrac12F_{ab}\hat E^a \wedge \hat E^b$, which $\omega^4{}_a \wedge \hat E^a = -\omega_{4a} \wedge
\hat E^a = \tfrac12F_{ab}\hat E^b \wedge \hat E^a$ cancels; and $\omega^a{}_b \wedge \hat E^b + \omega^a{}_4 \wedge \hat E^4 = \tfrac12F^a{}_b
\hat E^4 \wedge \hat E^b + \tfrac12F^a{}_b\hat E^b \wedge \hat E^4 = 0$, as $d\hat E^a = 0$ requires. The script checks all five
components for a general $A$:

{{< sage exr-kkf-cartan >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The coefficient $-\tfrac18$ comes from two contributions of opposite sign. The second exercise separates them and checks the
sum with explicit matrices.

::: {#exr-kkf-gamma-contraction}
#### Two contributions to the Pauli term

Show that the $\omega_{ab}(\hat E_4)$ part of $\tfrac14\Gamma^C\omega_{ABC}\Gamma^A\Gamma^B$ gives $+\tfrac18F_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b\Gamma^4$
and the $\omega_{4a}(\hat E_b)$ part $-\tfrac14F_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b\Gamma^4$. Check the total with Sage for a random $F_{ab}$, and show
that $e^{-i\pi\gamma_5/4}\big(\tfrac18F_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma_5\big)e^{-i\pi\gamma_5/4} = -\tfrac18\sigma^{ab}F_{ab}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The first part is $\tfrac14\Gamma^4\cdot\tfrac12F_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b = \tfrac18F_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b\Gamma^4$, since $\Gamma^4$ commutes with
$\gamma^a\gamma^b$. The second is $\tfrac14\gamma^c(\omega_{4ac}\Gamma^4\gamma^a + \omega_{a4c}\gamma^a\Gamma^4) = \tfrac18F_{ac}\gamma^c(\gamma^a\Gamma^4 -
\Gamma^4\gamma^a) = \tfrac14F_{ac}\gamma^c\gamma^a\Gamma^4 = -\tfrac14F_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b\Gamma^4$. The sum is $-\tfrac18F_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b\Gamma^4$.
For the rotation, $e^{-i\pi\gamma_5/4}Xe^{-i\pi\gamma_5/4} = Xe^{-i\pi\gamma_5/2} = -iX\gamma_5$ for $X$ commuting with $\gamma_5$, and
$F_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b = -iF_{ab}\sigma^{ab}$:

{{< sage exr-kkf-gamma-contraction >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Dirac operator must be self-adjoint for the action to be real. The third exercise checks that the Pauli term does not
spoil this.

::: {#exr-kkf-hermitian}
#### A real action

With $\bar\psi = \psi^\dagger\gamma^0$, show that $\bar\psi\,\tfrac18F_{ab}\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma_5\psi$ is real for real $F_{ab}$, and that
$\bar\psi\gamma_5\partial_y\psi$ is real up to a total $y$-derivative. Conclude that the action $\int d^4x\,dy\,\bar\psi\,i\Gamma^A\nabla_A\psi$ is
real on the circle.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(\bar\psi M\psi)^* = \bar\psi\gamma^0M^\dagger\gamma^0\psi$. For $M = \gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma_5$ with $a \neq b$: $\gamma^0(\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma_5)^\dagger\gamma^0 =
\gamma^0\gamma_5\gamma^{b\dagger}\gamma^{a\dagger}\gamma^0 = -\gamma_5\gamma^b\gamma^a = -\gamma^b\gamma^a\gamma_5 = \gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma_5$, using $\gamma^0\gamma^{\mu\dagger}\gamma^0 = \gamma^\mu$
and $\gamma^0\gamma_5 = -\gamma_5\gamma^0$; so the term is real. For $M = \gamma_5\partial_y$: $(\bar\psi\gamma_5\partial_y\psi)^* = -\partial_y\bar\psi\,\gamma_5\psi =
\bar\psi\gamma_5\partial_y\psi - \partial_y(\bar\psi\gamma_5\psi)$, and the derivative integrates to zero around the circle. The four-dimensional
part is the usual real Dirac action up to total derivatives, so the whole action is real, which is the statement that the
operator is formally self-adjoint (@def-dirac-operator).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Expanding in modes turns the operator into an infinite set of four-dimensional Dirac operators. The proposition is the
fermionic version of @prp-kk-modes, and it contains the magnetic moment of the modes.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-kkf-mode-equation}
#### The tower of a five-dimensional fermion

Let $\psi(x, y) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}\psi_n(x)e^{iny/R}$ solve $i\Gamma^A\nabla_A\psi = 0$ on the ansatz of @def-kkf-five-dirac, and set
$\chi_n = e^{i\pi s_n\gamma_5/4}\psi_n$ with $s_n = \operatorname{sign}n$ ($s_0 = 1$). Then
$$
\Big(i\gamma^\mu(\mathring\nabla_\mu - iq_nA_\mu) - m_n - \frac{s_n}{8}\sigma^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}\Big)\chi_n = 0, \qquad q_n = \frac nR,
\quad m_n = \frac{|n|}{R} .
$$ {#eq-kkf-mode-equation}
Each mode is a four-dimensional Dirac fermion of mass $m_n$ and charge $q_n$, the charges and masses of the bosonic tower
(@def-charge-quantisation, @def-kk-mass), with a Pauli coupling of fixed strength. For $n \neq 0$ the total magnetic moment
is half the value $g = 2$ of the Dirac equation (@thm-dq-pauli-limit): the massive modes have the gyromagnetic ratio $g = 1$
[@duff1998gyromagnetic, Sec. 2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The zero mode is neutral, yet the Pauli term survives for it. The first example states what this means for the lightest fermion of the tower.

::: {#exm-kkf-zero-mode}
#### A neutral fermion with a magnetic moment

For $n = 0$, @eq-kkf-mode-equation is $(i\gamma^\mu\mathring\nabla_\mu - \tfrac18\sigma^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu})\chi_0 = 0$: a massless, neutral
Dirac fermion with a magnetic dipole coupling to the Kaluza-Klein photon, like a neutron without a mass. The coupling comes
from the spin connection alone; a fermion that is a zero mode of the circle cannot be the electron, which is charged
(@exr-kkr-charge-ratio).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The first massive level contains a particle and its antiparticle. The second example reads off their charges and shows that
they are the two modes $n = \pm1$.

::: {#exm-kkf-first-level}
#### The level $|n| = 1$

The modes $n = 1$ and $n = -1$ have the same mass $1/R$ and opposite charges $\pm1/R$, and the opposite signs $s_{\pm1}$ of their
Pauli terms follow the signs of their charges. They are exchanged by the reflection $y \to -y$, which is charge conjugation
on the tower (@exm-charge-conjugation); a five-dimensional Dirac fermion therefore gives at each level $|n| \geq 1$ a charged
four-dimensional Dirac fermion and its antiparticle, with masses at the Planck scale when $R$ is fixed by $\alpha$
(@prp-kk-radius).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The value $g = 1$ is a prediction that distinguishes Kaluza-Klein states from elementary particles. The third example
explains why it does not contradict the general arguments for $g = 2$.

::: {#exm-kkf-g-factor}
#### Why $g = 1$ is allowed

Tree-level unitarity of a charged particle coupled to a photon up to energies $E \gg M/|Q|$ requires $g = 2$; Kaluza-Klein states
have $M \sim |Q|$ in Planck units (@exr-kkr-charge-ratio), so the window $M_{\rm Pl} > E > M/|Q|$ in which the argument applies
is empty [@duff1998gyromagnetic, Sec. 2]. The value $g = 1$ holds for the massive modes of every field reduced on a circle,
of any spin, and in any dimension [@duff1998gyromagnetic, Sec. 2, eqs. (1)-(5)]; for the spinor it is the combination of the
minimal coupling and the Pauli term of @eq-kkf-mode-equation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The chiral rotation that turns the five-dimensional equation into a Dirac equation with a positive mass depends on the
sign of $n$. The first exercise performs it for both signs.

::: {#exr-kkf-chiral-rotation}
#### The rotation for both signs

Insert $\psi_n e^{iny/R}$ into @eq-kkf-dirac and show that $\psi_n$ satisfies $\big(i\gamma^\mu D_\mu - i\tfrac nR\gamma_5 + \tfrac18F_{ab}
\gamma^a\gamma^b\gamma_5\big)\psi_n = 0$ with $D_\mu = \mathring\nabla_\mu - i\tfrac nRA_\mu$. Then derive @eq-kkf-mode-equation for $n > 0$ and for
$n < 0$, and explain why the zero mode can be rotated either way.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$-\gamma_5\partial_y$ gives $-i\tfrac nR\gamma_5$ and $-\tfrac i8F\gamma\gamma\,i\gamma_5 = \tfrac18F\gamma\gamma\gamma_5$. Write $\psi_n = e^{-i\pi s\gamma_5/4}\chi$ and
multiply by $e^{-i\pi s\gamma_5/4}$: the kinetic term is unchanged, since $\gamma_5$ anticommutes with $\gamma^\mu$, while every term $X$
commuting with $\gamma_5$ becomes $Xe^{-i\pi s\gamma_5/2} = -isX\gamma_5$. So $-i\tfrac nR\gamma_5 \to -s\tfrac nR = -\tfrac{|n|}{R}$ and
$\tfrac18F\gamma\gamma\gamma_5 \to -\tfrac{is}{8}F\gamma\gamma = -\tfrac s8\sigma^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}$ (@exr-kkf-gamma-contraction). For $n = 0$ there is no
mass, and a chiral rotation of a massless fermion is a change of variables: either sign of $s_0$ gives an equivalent
equation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The gyromagnetic ratio is read off in the non-relativistic limit. The second exercise does this by comparing the Pauli term
with the moment of the Dirac equation.

::: {#exr-kkf-g-value}
#### Reading off $g$

For a static magnetic field, $\sigma^{ij}F_{ij} = -2\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec B$. Show that a term $-\tfrac{\mu'}{2}\sigma^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu}$ in the
Dirac equation adds the energy $-\mu'\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec B$ at rest. With the convention $D_\mu = \partial_\mu - iq_nA_\mu$, so that the
charge in the sense of @def-dq-minimal-coupling is $-q_n$, find the Dirac moment of the mode $n > 0$, add the Pauli moment and
compute $g$ with @eq-dq-pauli.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At rest the upper components satisfy $E\varphi = (m - \mu'\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec B)\varphi$, since $-\tfrac{\mu'}{2}(-2\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec B)$ enters
$(i\gamma^\mu D_\mu - m + \mu'\vec\Sigma\cdot\vec B)\psi = 0$: the moment is $\mu'\vec\Sigma$. The minimal coupling gives the moment
$\tfrac{(-q_n)}{2m_n}\vec\Sigma = -\tfrac12\vec\Sigma$ ($g = 2$ for the charge $-q_n$, @thm-dq-pauli-limit), and the Pauli term $\tfrac18 =
\tfrac{\mu'}{2}$ adds $\mu' = \tfrac14$. The total $-\tfrac14\vec\Sigma$ is half the Dirac moment: $g = 1$. For $n < 0$ both the charge and the
sign $s_n$ change, and $g = 1$ again.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Halving the magnetic moment changes the Landau levels of @fig-kkf-zeeman. The third exercise computes them with Sage in the
Pauli approximation.

::: {#exr-kkf-landau}
#### Landau levels with $g = 1$

In the Pauli equation the levels in a constant field are $E - m = \omega(N + \tfrac12) - \tfrac12g\omega s$, $N = 0, 1, \dots$, $s =
\pm\tfrac12$, with $\omega = |q|B/m$. With Sage, list the five lowest levels for $g = 1$ and $g = 2$ with their degeneracies in
$(N, s)$, and find which coincidences of $g = 2$ are lifted when $g = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $g = 2$ the levels are $\omega N'$ with $N' = N + \tfrac12 - s$: $0$ once and every $N' \geq 1$ twice, since $(N, s) = (N', \tfrac12)$
and $(N' - 1, -\tfrac12)$ coincide. For $g = 1$ they are $\omega(N + \tfrac14)$ and $\omega(N + \tfrac34)$, all distinct:

{{< sage exr-kkf-landau >}}

The pairing of the levels that $g = 2$ produces (@fig-kkf-zeeman) is absent for Kaluza-Klein states, a
signature by which a tower of charged fermions could in principle be recognised.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### The fermion tower

A fermion need not be periodic around the circle: only bilinears such as the current must be, so a spinor may change sign.
The figure places the modes of both spin structures in the plane of charge and mass; the interactive version varies the
twist continuously.

![Charges and masses of the Kaluza-Klein modes on a circle of radius $R$. Bosons and periodic fermions (circles) have
momenta $k = n$; antiperiodic fermions (triangles) have $k = n + \tfrac12$. Every mode has charge $k/R$ and mass $|k|/R$, so all
lie on the lines $|q| = m$ (@def-kkf-fermion-tower); in units of $1/(2R)$ the bosonic charges are even and the antiperiodic
fermionic charges odd (@prp-kkf-twist-charge). Generated by `figures/kkf-charge-mass.sage`; the interactive version shows the
twists $\alpha = 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75$.](figures/kkf-charge-mass.svg){#fig-kkf-charge-mass width=70%}

{{< interactive kkf-charge-mass 460 >}}

The definition allows the general phase of @def-scherk-schwarz-twist, which includes both spin structures. It assigns to every
mode a mass and a charge exactly as for scalars.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-kkf-fermion-tower}
#### Fermion tower

A fermion on $M^4 \times S^1$ with **twist** $\alpha \in [0, 1)$ satisfies $\psi(x, y + 2\pi R) = e^{2\pi i\alpha}\psi(x, y)$, and its
**fermion tower** is the expansion
$$
\psi(x, y) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}\psi_n(x)\,e^{i(n + \alpha)y/R} ,
$$ {#eq-kkf-twisted-modes}
with four-dimensional Dirac fermions $\psi_n$ of mass $m_n = |n + \alpha|/R$ and charge $q_n = (n + \alpha)/R$ under the
Kaluza-Klein $U(1)$. The value $\alpha = 0$ is the periodic and $\alpha = \tfrac12$ the antiperiodic spin structure of the circle
(@exm-spd-spin-circle); other values are Scherk-Schwarz twists by a global phase symmetry [@perezlorenzana2005, Sec. IV.D,
eqs. (75)-(77)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
With the periodic structure the fermion tower is the bosonic one. The first example states this and what it means for
supersymmetry.

::: {#exm-kkf-periodic-tower}
#### The periodic structure

For $\alpha = 0$ the masses $|n|/R$ and charges $n/R$ are those of @fig-kk-tower, level by level, and there is a massless zero
mode (@prp-kkf-mode-equation). A five-dimensional supermultiplet on the periodic circle therefore gives degenerate bosonic and
fermionic towers: the reduction on a circle with the periodic structure preserves all the supersymmetry, the massive levels
forming massive supermultiplets.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The antiperiodic structure shifts every momentum by a half. The second example describes the resulting tower, which has no
zero mode.

::: {#exm-kkf-antiperiodic-tower}
#### The antiperiodic structure

For $\alpha = \tfrac12$ the masses are $\tfrac{1}{2R}, \tfrac{1}{2R}, \tfrac{3}{2R}, \tfrac{3}{2R}, \dots$, each level twice degenerate ($n$ and $-n -
1$), with charges $\pm\tfrac{1}{2R}, \pm\tfrac{3}{2R}, \dots$: half-integer multiples of the unit $1/R$ of the bosonic tower
(@fig-kkf-charge-mass, @exr-kkr-charge-twisted). The lightest fermions have mass $1/(2R)$, the largest gap any twist can open
(@exm-spd-twist-circle).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Giving the bosons and the fermions of a supermultiplet different twists breaks supersymmetry. The third example is the
Scherk-Schwarz mechanism in its simplest form.

::: {#exm-kkf-scherk-schwarz}
#### Supersymmetry breaking by a twist

Let the bosons of a five-dimensional supermultiplet be periodic and the fermions twisted by $\alpha$, the twist being a
global symmetry that acts differently on the two, as in @def-vcr-scherk-schwarz-twist. The bosonic zero modes stay massless and
the fermionic ones get the mass $\min(\alpha, 1 - \alpha)/R$, largest for $\alpha = \tfrac12$; the whole tower is split by the
same shift (@exr-spd-scherk-schwarz-gap). For the gravitino (@def-gravitino) this is a mass $1/(2R)$ set by the radius alone:
supersymmetry is broken at the compactification scale [@perezlorenzana2005, Sec. IV.D].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The bosonic and fermionic towers of @fig-kkf-charge-mass interleave. The first exercise counts the modes of both with Sage below a given
energy.

::: {#exr-kkf-tower-count}
#### Counting states below an energy

With Sage, count the modes with mass below $E$ for $\alpha = 0$ and $\alpha = \tfrac12$, for $ER = 0.3, 1.2, 2.7, 10.4$, and show that the
counts are $2\lfloor ER\rfloor + 1$ and $2\lfloor ER + \tfrac12\rfloor$. How do they compare for $ER \gg 1$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|n| < ER$ gives $2\lfloor ER\rfloor + 1$ modes (@exr-kkr-int-counting), and $|n + \tfrac12| < ER$ gives $n = -\lfloor ER + \tfrac12\rfloor,
\dots, \lfloor ER + \tfrac12\rfloor - 1$, that is $2\lfloor ER + \tfrac12\rfloor$:

{{< sage exr-kkf-tower-count >}}

The difference is at most one: at high energy the two towers have the same density $2R$ of states per unit mass, and the
spin structure is invisible, as the five-dimensional density of states must be.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Bosons and fermions of a supermultiplet contribute to the vacuum energy with opposite signs. The second exercise uses the
Casimir energies of @prp-ren-casimir-circle to see what the twist does to the radius.

::: {#exr-kkf-casimir}
#### The vacuum energy of a twisted supermultiplet

Take a five-dimensional multiplet with four real massless scalars and one massless Dirac fermion. Using @prp-ren-casimir-circle
(a Dirac fermion counts $-4$ times a scalar with its own boundary condition), compute the one-loop vacuum energy for periodic
fermions and for antiperiodic fermions. Is the circle pushed to grow or to shrink?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $c = \tfrac{3\zeta(5)}{4\pi^2\ell^4}$, a periodic scalar contributes $-c$ and an antiperiodic one $+\tfrac{15}{16}c$. Periodic fermions:
$4(-c) - 4(-c) = 0$, the supersymmetric cancellation. Antiperiodic fermions: $4(-c) - 4\cdot\tfrac{15}{16}c = -\tfrac{31}{4}c$. The energy is
negative and grows in magnitude as $\ell^{-4}$ when $\ell$ decreases, so the force pushes the circle to shrink: breaking
supersymmetry by the twist makes the radius unstable at one loop, as in @ponton2001casimir.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The twist of a fermion is a holonomy, so it can also come from a background gauge field. The third exercise combines the
two for a fermion that is charged under a five-dimensional $U(1)$.

::: {#exr-kkf-wilson-line}
#### Twist and Wilson line

A periodic five-dimensional fermion of charge $e'$ under a five-dimensional gauge field $B_M$ (not the Kaluza-Klein field) sees a
constant $B_y = \theta/(e'R)$, so that $\partial_y$ is replaced by $D_y = \partial_y + ie'B_y$. Show that its masses are those of the tower of
@def-kkf-fermion-tower with $\alpha = \theta$ modulo $1$, and that the field redefinition $\psi' = e^{ie'B_yy}\psi$ removes $B_y$ at the price of
the twist. Which quantity is gauge invariant?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$D_y$ acts on $e^{iny/R}$ as $i(n + \theta)/R$, so the masses are $|n + \theta|/R$, those of the twisted tower with $\alpha \equiv \theta$. Since
$\partial_y\psi' = e^{i\theta y/R}D_y\psi$, the field $\psi'$ obeys the equation without $B_y$, and $\psi'(y + 2\pi R) = e^{2\pi i\theta}\psi'(y)$. The
invariant is the holonomy $e^{ie'\oint B} = e^{2\pi i\theta}$ (@exm-spd-twist-gauge): the twist and the Wilson line are one quantity, as in
the Hosotani mechanism [@perezlorenzana2005, Sec. IV.D].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

The charges of an antiperiodic fermion are half-integers in the bosonic unit. The proposition interprets this as a statement
about the gauge group of the circle.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-kkf-twist-charge}
#### Charges of the twisted tower

The Kaluza-Klein $U(1)$, generated by $\partial_y$, acts on the mode $\psi_n$ of @eq-kkf-twisted-modes by $e^{i(n + \alpha)\epsilon/R}$ for the
shift $y \to y + \epsilon$. All charges are multiples of $1/R$ if and only if $\alpha = 0$. For $\alpha = \tfrac12$ the shift by one full
period $\epsilon = 2\pi R$ acts as $(-1)^F$, $+1$ on bosons and $-1$ on fermions, the charges are multiples of $1/(2R)$, odd for fermions
and even for bosons, and the group that acts faithfully is the double cover of the circle of period $2\pi R$. For rational $\alpha = p/k$
in lowest terms the charges are multiples of $1/(kR)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A fermion pair is a boson. The first example checks that it carries an integer charge, as a bosonic mode must.

::: {#exm-kkf-pair-charge}
#### Pairs of fermions

Two antiperiodic modes $n_1$, $n_2$ have total charge $(n_1 + n_2 + 1)/R$, an integer multiple of $1/R$, and their product $e^{i(n_1 + n_2 +
1)y/R}$ is periodic: every bilinear $\bar\psi\Gamma\psi$ of an antiperiodic fermion is an ordinary function on the circle, as the action
requires. A single fermion is never a function on the circle, which is why the half-integer charges are allowed.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The sign $(-1)^F$ is a rotation in disguise. The second example connects it with the rotation by $2\pi$ of
@sec-spin-groups.

::: {#exm-kkf-fermion-number}
#### $(-1)^F$ from geometry

The shift by $2\pi R$ around a circle of an antiperiodic spinor is the same sign $-1$ as the rotation by $2\pi$ of a spinor
(@def-spin-group): on the antiperiodic structure the spinor bundle of the circle is the Möbius bundle of @exm-kkr-periodicity-half,
and translation once around acts as $(-1)^F$. On the thermal circle of @exr-kkr-truncation-thermal the same sign gives the
antiperiodicity of fermions in imaginary time, which is the trace with $(-1)^F$ removed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

A twist by a rational phase leads to a cover of higher order. The third example gives the case $\alpha = \tfrac13$, which appears
in orbifolds of order three.

::: {#exm-kkf-rational-twist}
#### The twist $\tfrac13$

For $\alpha = \tfrac13$ the charges are $(3n + 1)/(3R)$: $\tfrac{1}{3R}, -\tfrac{2}{3R}, \tfrac{4}{3R}, \dots$, all congruent to $1$ modulo $3$ in the unit
$1/(3R)$. Three such fermions can combine into a periodic state, and the group acting faithfully on all fields is the triple
cover of the circle; the masses $\tfrac{1}{3R}, \tfrac{2}{3R}, \tfrac{4}{3R}, \tfrac{5}{3R}, \dots$ are not symmetric under $q \to -q$, since the conjugate
field has the twist $\tfrac23$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The proposition rests on a property of the exponential function. The first exercise proves the statement about the periodic case $\alpha = 0$.

::: {#exr-kkf-integer-charges}
#### When all charges are integers

Prove that the charges $(n + \alpha)/R$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, are all integer multiples of $1/R$ if and only if $\alpha = 0$ (for $\alpha \in [0, 1)$),
and that $e^{2\pi i(n + \alpha)} = 1$ for one $n$ if and only if it holds for all $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(n + \alpha)R/R = n + \alpha \in \mathbb{Z}$ iff $\alpha \in \mathbb{Z}$, and $\alpha \in [0, 1)$ leaves $\alpha = 0$. Since $e^{2\pi in} = 1$, $e^{2\pi i(n + \alpha)} =
e^{2\pi i\alpha}$ for every $n$, so the condition does not depend on $n$; it is the periodicity condition of @prp-kk-periodicity
applied to $n + \alpha$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A theory with fermions of several twists has a smallest common unit of charge. The second exercise computes it with Sage.

::: {#exr-kkf-common-unit}
#### The unit of charge of a spectrum

With Sage, for the sets of twists $\{0, \tfrac12\}$, $\{0, \tfrac13, \tfrac23\}$, $\{\tfrac12, \tfrac14\}$ and $\{0, \tfrac25\}$, find the largest $u$
such that every charge $(n + \alpha)/R$ is an integer multiple of $u/R$, and the order of the cover of the circle that acts
faithfully.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$u$ is $1/k$ with $k$ the least common multiple of the denominators of the twists (and $1$ for the periodic fields), and $k$ is
the order of the cover:

{{< sage exr-kkf-common-unit >}}

So $\{0, \tfrac12\}$ gives $u = \tfrac12$, the double cover of @prp-kkf-twist-charge; the others give $\tfrac13$, $\tfrac14$ and $\tfrac15$.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The proposition implies that charge conservation is compatible with any twist. The third exercise checks this on the cubic
coupling of a fermion pair to a boson.

::: {#exr-kkf-yukawa-modes}
#### A Yukawa coupling on the circle

For an antiperiodic fermion $\psi$ and a periodic real scalar $\Phi$, insert the mode expansions into $\int_0^{2\pi R}dy\,\Phi\bar\psi\psi$. Which
triples $(n_1, n_2, m)$ of modes of $\bar\psi$, $\psi$ and $\Phi$ couple, and why is the result consistent with the charges?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\bar\psi$ carries $e^{-i(n_1 + \frac12)y/R}$, $\psi$ carries $e^{i(n_2 + \frac12)y/R}$ and $\Phi$ carries $e^{imy/R}$; the integral is non-zero only when
$-n_1 + n_2 + m = 0$, that is $m = n_1 - n_2$. This is conservation of the Kaluza-Klein charge: $q(\psi_{n_2}) + q(\Phi_m) = q(\psi_{n_1})$, with the
half-integer parts cancelling between $\bar\psi$ and $\psi$, as in @exm-kkf-pair-charge.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

### No chirality from the circle

On the circle every four-dimensional mode has both chiralities, while on the orbifold $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$ one chirality of the zero
mode survives. The figure shows the zero mode on the orbifold when a bulk mass of the odd kind is present: it is pushed
towards one of the two fixed points.

![The chiral zero mode of a five-dimensional fermion on $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$ with the odd bulk mass $M\varepsilon(y)$, on the
fundamental domain $0 \leq y \leq \pi R$: the density $|f_0|^2 \propto e^{-2M|y|}$ for $MR = 0, \tfrac12, 1, 3$ and $-1$. For $M = 0$ the mode is
constant; for $MR \gg 1$ it is localised at the fixed point $y = 0$, for $M < 0$ at $y = \pi R$ (@prp-kkf-orbifold-zero-mode). The
normalisation and the massive spectrum $m_n^2 = M^2 + n^2/R^2$ are checked symbolically. Generated by
`figures/kkf-kink-zero-mode.sage`; the interactive version adds $MR = 2, 5, -3$.](figures/kkf-kink-zero-mode.svg){#fig-kkf-kink-zero-mode width=70%}

{{< interactive kkf-kink-zero-mode 460 >}}

The first statement says that nothing on the circle distinguishes left from right. It is the circle case of
@thm-chirality-no-go and @exr-spd-nogo-odd, stated for the four-dimensional physics.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-kkf-vectorlike}
#### The circle gives Dirac fermions

A five-dimensional fermion on $M^4 \times S^1$, with any twist, any constant gauge background and any bulk mass $M\bar\psi\psi$,
gives at every level a four-dimensional Dirac fermion: left- and right-handed components with the same charges under every
gauge group. The four-dimensional spectrum is vector-like. With a bulk mass the masses are $\sqrt{M^2 + (n + \alpha)^2/R^2}$
[@perezlorenzana2005, Sec. III.A, eqs. (38)-(40)].
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

The charges under the Kaluza-Klein $U(1)$ are those of the tower. The first example shows that both chiralities carry them.

::: {#exm-kkf-vector-charges}
#### Both chiralities carry the charge

On the mode $n$ the covariant derivative $\mathring\nabla_\mu - iq_nA_\mu$ of @eq-kkf-mode-equation acts on both components $P_L\chi_n$ and
$P_R\chi_n$, since the derivative $\partial_y$ and the frame @eq-kkf-frame do not involve $\gamma_5$. A left-handed fermion of charge $q_n$
is accompanied by a right-handed one of the same charge: the charged spectrum is that of electrodynamics, not of the weak
interactions.
:::

A bulk mass is allowed on the circle and adds to the internal mass. The second example writes the spectrum.

::: {#exm-kkf-bulk-mass}
#### A bulk mass

With $(i\Gamma^A\partial_A - M)\psi = 0$ on flat $M^4 \times S^1$, each mode $\psi_n$ satisfies $(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - i\tfrac nR\gamma_5 - M)\psi_n = 0$;
squaring gives $(\Box + M^2 + n^2/R^2)\psi_n = 0$, so the masses are $\sqrt{M^2 + n^2/R^2}$ and even the zero mode is a massive Dirac fermion
[@perezlorenzana2005, eq. (40)]. A five-dimensional mass cannot be forbidden by a symmetry that acts on the circle alone.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Standard Model is not vector-like, and this is the obstacle. The third example states it in the form in which it ended
the hope of a fully geometric unification.

::: {#exm-kkf-standard-model}
#### Why the circle cannot give the Standard Model

In the Standard Model the left-handed quarks and leptons are $SU(2)$ doublets and the right-handed ones singlets
(@exm-anomaly-standard-model). A theory whose four-dimensional fermions all come with both chiralities in the same
representation can never produce this: the electron would come with a right-handed partner in a doublet. The same holds for
any internal space with an isometry gauge group and no further gauge fields (@thm-chirality-no-go); the argument, due to
Witten, is what led to adding gauge fields in higher dimensions [@duff1994, p. 18; @chatzistavrakidis2007eym, Sec. 1].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The spectrum with a bulk mass can be found by squaring the operator. The first exercise does this and reads off the masses.

::: {#exr-kkf-bulk-spectrum}
#### Squaring the operator

Show that $(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - i\lambda\gamma_5 - M)(-i\gamma^\nu\partial_\nu + i\lambda\gamma_5 - M)$ equals $\Box + \lambda^2 + M^2$ times the identity
up to a term that vanishes, and deduce the masses of @prp-kkf-vectorlike with $\lambda = (n + \alpha)/R$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Expanding: $(i\gamma\cdot\partial)(-i\gamma\cdot\partial) = \Box$; the cross terms $i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\,i\lambda\gamma_5 + (-i\lambda\gamma_5)(-i\gamma^\nu\partial_\nu) =
-\lambda(\gamma^\mu\gamma_5 + \gamma_5\gamma^\mu)\partial_\mu = 0$; $(-i\lambda\gamma_5)(i\lambda\gamma_5) = \lambda^2$; the terms linear in $M$ are $-M(i\gamma\cdot\partial - i\lambda\gamma_5) -
M(-i\gamma\cdot\partial + i\lambda\gamma_5) = 0$; and $M^2$. So any solution satisfies $(\Box + \lambda^2 + M^2)\psi_n = 0$, a mass $\sqrt{M^2 + (n +
\alpha)^2/R^2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A vector-like spectrum cannot have a gauge anomaly. The second exercise checks the cubic anomaly of a truncated tower with
Sage.

::: {#exr-kkf-anomaly}
#### No anomaly from a vector-like tower

Write every Dirac mode $n$ of charge $q_n = (n + \alpha)/R$ as a left-handed Weyl fermion of charge $q_n$ and a left-handed Weyl fermion of
charge $-q_n$ (the conjugate of the right-handed part). With Sage, compute $\sum q^3$ and $\sum q$ over the left-handed fermions of the
modes $|n| \leq N$ for several $\alpha$ and $N$, and explain the result with @def-anomaly.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every charge appears with its opposite, so both sums vanish identically, for every truncation and every twist:

{{< sage exr-kkf-anomaly >}}

The cancellation is mode by mode, between the two chiralities of one Dirac fermion; it is the arithmetic form of
@prp-kkf-vectorlike. A chiral spectrum, such as the zero modes of an orbifold, is needed before an anomaly can arise.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The reflection of the circle maps the theory to itself only if it acts on spinors too. The third exercise finds the action
and shows that it forbids the bulk mass.

::: {#exr-kkf-reflection}
#### The reflection and the bulk mass

Show that $\psi(x, y) \to \eta\gamma_5\psi(x, -y)$, $\eta = \pm1$, maps solutions of $(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - \gamma_5\partial_y - M)\psi = 0$ to solutions of
the same equation with $M \to -M$. Conclude that a bulk mass is odd under the reflection, and find how the term $\bar\psi\psi$ transforms.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Let $\psi'(y) = \eta\gamma_5\psi(-y)$ and $\mathcal D = i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - \gamma_5\partial_y$. Then $i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi' = -\eta\gamma_5(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\psi)(-y)$,
and, since $\partial_y[\psi(-y)] = -(\partial_y\psi)(-y)$, $-\gamma_5\partial_y\psi' = \eta(\partial_y\psi)(-y) = -\eta\gamma_5(-\gamma_5\partial_y\psi)(-y)$. So $\mathcal D\psi' =
-\eta\gamma_5(\mathcal D\psi)(-y) = -\eta\gamma_5M\psi(-y) = -M\psi'$. The equation holds with $-M$: the reflection is a symmetry only if $M$ changes sign. Indeed $\bar\psi' \psi' =
\psi^\dagger\gamma_5\gamma^0\gamma_5\psi = -\bar\psi\psi$ at the reflected point: the mass term is odd [@perezlorenzana2005, eq. (40) and the
following paragraph].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

On the orbifold the reflection becomes a condition on the fields, and an odd mass must be a step function. The proposition
describes the result: a single chiral zero mode, which a mass localises.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-kkf-orbifold-zero-mode}
#### Chiral zero modes on $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$

On $M^4 \times S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$, impose $\psi(x, -y) = \eta\gamma_5\psi(x, y)$ with $\eta = \pm1$ and allow the odd bulk mass $M\varepsilon(y)$, $\varepsilon(y) =
\operatorname{sign}y$ on $(-\pi R, \pi R)$. Then the four-dimensional spectrum consists of one massless Weyl fermion, right-handed for
$\eta = 1$ and left-handed for $\eta = -1$, with profile
$$
f_0(y) = \sqrt{\frac{2\eta M}{1 - e^{-2\pi\eta MR}}}\;e^{-\eta M|y|}\quad(M \neq 0) ,
$$ {#eq-kkf-orbifold-zero-mode}
normalised by $\int_0^{\pi R}|f_0|^2dy = 1$, and of Dirac fermions with masses $m_n = \sqrt{M^2 + n^2/R^2}$, $n \geq 1$.
Gauge fields must have $A_\mu$ even and $A_y$ odd, so the zero mode keeps the charges of the five-dimensional fermion
[@perezlorenzana2005, Secs. III.A, IV.C and V.1, eqs. (40), (71)-(72), (98)-(101)].
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

#### No bulk mass

For $M = 0$, $f_0 = 1/\sqrt{\pi R}$ is constant, the right-handed zero mode for $\eta = 1$; the massive modes pair $\cos(ny/R)$ in $\psi_R$
with $\sin(ny/R)$ in $\psi_L$ into Dirac fermions of mass $n/R$ (@exr-spd-s1z2-tower). The tower is that of the circle with half the
modes removed: one chirality of the zero mode and one Dirac fermion per level instead of two.

A large mass concentrates the zero mode at one end of the interval. The second example quantifies the localisation shown
in @fig-kkf-kink-zero-mode.

::: {#exm-kkf-localisation}
#### Localisation at a fixed point

For $\eta = 1$ and $MR \gg 1$, $|f_0|^2 \approx 2Me^{-2My}$: the mode lives within $1/M$ of $y = 0$, and a fermion with $M < 0$ lives at $y =
\pi R$. Fermions of different masses sit at different places along the fifth dimension, and the overlap of their profiles controls
their couplings: this is the field-theory model of matter localised on a brane at a fixed point [@perezlorenzana2005, Sec. V.1,
eqs. (98)-(103)], the setting of the branes of @exm-vcp-orbifold-interval.
:::

The orbifold condition acts on gauge fields as well. The third example lists the parities that keep the gauge symmetry of the
zero mode.

::: {#exm-kkf-orbifold-gauge}
#### The gauge field on the orbifold

For $D_M\psi$ to transform like $\psi$, $D_\mu = \partial_\mu + A_\mu$ must be even and $D_y = \partial_y + A_y$ odd: $A_\mu(x, -y) = A_\mu(x, y)$ and
$A_y(x, -y) = -A_y(x, y)$. The zero mode of $A_\mu$ is a four-dimensional gauge field, and $A_y$ has no zero mode, so no massless scalar
accompanies it; a parity matrix $P$ acting on gauge indices, $A_\mu \to PA_\mu P^{-1}$, can in addition break the gauge group to the
subgroup commuting with $P$ [@perezlorenzana2005, Sec. IV.C, eqs. (69)-(72)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The normalisation of the zero mode and the fraction of it near the fixed point are elementary integrals. The first exercise
computes them with Sage.

::: {#exr-kkf-kink-norm}
#### Normalising the zero mode

With Sage, verify the normalisation @eq-kkf-orbifold-zero-mode for $\eta = 1$, compute the fraction of $\int_0^{\pi R}|f_0|^2dy$ within $y <
R/10$ for $MR = 1, 10, 100$, and find the limit of $f_0$ as $M \to 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\int_0^{\pi R}e^{-2My}dy = \tfrac{1 - e^{-2\pi MR}}{2M}$, so the prefactor squared is $\tfrac{2M}{1 - e^{-2\pi MR}}$, as in
@eq-kkf-orbifold-zero-mode. The fraction within $R/10$ is $\tfrac{1 - e^{-MR/5}}{1 - e^{-2\pi MR}}$:

{{< sage exr-kkf-kink-norm >}}

For $MR = 100$ almost all of the mode lies within a tenth of the radius of the fixed point; as $M \to 0$ the profile tends to the constant
$1/\sqrt{\pi R}$ of @exm-kkf-orbifold-massless.
:::

The massive spectrum follows from the first-order equations with the boundary conditions imposed by the parity. The second
exercise derives it.

::: {#exr-kkf-massive-orbifold}
#### The massive modes

On $0 < y < \pi R$ write $\psi = f(y)\chi_R(x) + g(y)\chi_L(x)$ for $\eta = 1$, where $\chi_L + \chi_R$ is a Dirac fermion of mass $m$, so that
$i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\chi_R = m\chi_L$ and $i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu\chi_L = m\chi_R$. Show that $(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu - \gamma_5\partial_y - M)\psi = 0$ gives $(\partial_y +
M)f = mg$ and $(-\partial_y + M)g = mf$ (compare @perezlorenzana2005 [eq. (100)]). Using that $g$ is odd, so $g(0) = g(\pi R) = 0$, show that $f'' = (M^2 - m^2)f$ with $f' + Mf = 0$ at both ends,
and find $m_n^2 = M^2 + n^2/R^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The $\chi_R$ component of the equation is $mg - f' - Mf = 0$ and the $\chi_L$ component $mf + g' - Mg = 0$. From the first, $g = (f' + Mf)/m$,
and the second gives $(-\partial_y + M)(f' + Mf) = m^2f$, i.e. $f'' = (M^2 - m^2)f$. The conditions
$g = 0$ at the ends are $f' + Mf = 0$ there. With $k^2 = m^2 - M^2$, $f = \cos(ky) - \tfrac Mk\sin(ky)$ satisfies the condition at $0$, and
at $\pi R$ it gives $-(k + M^2/k)\sin(k\pi R) = 0$, so $k = n/R$ with $n \geq 1$ and $m_n^2 = M^2 + n^2/R^2$. The case $m = 0$ is the zero mode,
$f' + Mf = 0$ everywhere.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Two fermions localised at the two ends couple to a field spread along the interval only through the overlap of their
profiles. The third exercise estimates the resulting small coupling with Sage.

::: {#exr-kkf-overlap}
#### A hierarchy from overlaps

A left-handed zero mode with profile $\propto e^{-M_1y}$ and a right-handed one with $\propto e^{+M_2y}$ (localised at $y = \pi R$) couple to a
constant scalar through $\lambda\int_0^{\pi R}f_1f_2\,dy$ with normalised profiles. With Sage, compute the effective coupling for $M_1 = M_2 =
M$ and $MR = 1, 5, 10$, and show that it falls like $e^{-\pi MR}$ for large $MR$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $f_1 = \sqrt{\tfrac{2M}{1 - e^{-2\pi MR}}}e^{-My}$ and $f_2 = \sqrt{\tfrac{2M}{1 - e^{-2\pi MR}}}e^{M(y - \pi R)}$, the overlap is $\tfrac{2M}{1 - e^{-2\pi
MR}}\pi Re^{-\pi MR}$:

{{< sage exr-kkf-overlap >}}

An order-one ratio of masses gives an exponentially small coupling: separating fermions along the fifth dimension produces
hierarchies of Yukawa couplings without small parameters [@perezlorenzana2005, Sec. V.1].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### The fermion tower on the torus

The internal space of a realistic reduction has more than one dimension, and the simplest choice is a flat torus $T^n$, a
product of $n$ circles. Each circle contributes a Kaluza-Klein $U(1)$, a spin structure and possibly a twist, and the masses
of the four-dimensional fermions are the eigenvalues of the internal Dirac operator, which @prp-torus-spectrum computed for every
radius and twist. The figure shows the charges of the modes on the square torus for its four spin structures.

![The charge lattice of the fermion tower on the square torus $T^2$ with $R_1 = R_2 = R$. The mode with integers $(m_1, m_2)$ has
charges $q_i = (m_i + \alpha_i)/R$ under the two Kaluza-Klein $U(1)$s and mass $|q|$; the four spin structures $(\alpha_1,
\alpha_2) \in \{0, \tfrac12\}^2$ fill the four cosets of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ in $\tfrac12\mathbb{Z}^2$, and the dashed circles mark the lightest
massive level of each: $1/R$ for $(P, P)$, whose lightest level is massless, $1/(2R)$ for $(A, P)$ and $(P, A)$, $1/(\sqrt2R)$ for $(A, A)$
(@prp-kkf-torus-tower). Generated by `figures/kkf-torus-lattice.sage`; the interactive version adds Scherk-Schwarz twists that are not
spin structures.](figures/kkf-torus-lattice.svg){#fig-kkf-torus-lattice width=60%}

{{< interactive kkf-torus-lattice 460 >}}

The statement combines three results already proved: the splitting of the Dirac operator of a product into a four-dimensional
and an internal part (@exr-spd-branch-mass), the spectrum of the internal operator on the flat torus (@prp-torus-spectrum),
and the charges of a mode under the isometries of a circle (@def-kkf-fermion-tower). Nothing has to be computed again; what
is new is the reading of the internal spectrum as a four-dimensional particle content.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-kkf-torus-tower}
#### The fermion tower on the torus

Let $\Psi$ be a Dirac fermion in $4 + n$ dimensions on $M^4 \times T^n$, with radii $R_i$ and twists $\alpha_i \in [0, 1)$ as in
@def-scherk-schwarz-twist, and let $N = 2^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$. Then:

1. For every $m \in \mathbb{Z}^n$ there are $N$ four-dimensional Dirac fermions of mass $|k|$, $k_i = (m_i + \alpha_i)/R_i$, each with
   charge $k_i$ under the Kaluza-Klein $U(1)$ of the $i$-th circle. A mass level $\mu$ therefore contains $N\,\#\{m : |k| = \mu\}$
   Dirac fermions.
2. Massless fermions exist only if every $\alpha_i = 0$; there are then $N$ of them, uncharged. Of the $2^n$ spin structures
   ($\alpha_i \in \{0, \tfrac12\}$) only the periodic one has massless fermions, and with twists the lightest mass is
   $\big(\sum_i \|\alpha_i\|^2/R_i^2\big)^{1/2}$, where $\|\alpha\| = \min(\alpha, 1 - \alpha)$.
3. At every level the left- and right-handed components carry the same charges: the four-dimensional spectrum is vector-like.
   For even $n$ and a Weyl fermion in $4 + n$ dimensions every number above is halved, and the zero modes are $N/2$ left-handed
   and $N/2$ right-handed Weyl fermions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For the proof, write $\Psi = \sum_m\chi_m(x) \otimes e^{ik\cdot y}u$ with $u$ running over the $N$ eigenvectors of $-\gamma_K\cdot k$
(@prp-torus-spectrum): each eigenvector with eigenvalue $\pm|k|$ gives by @exr-spd-branch-mass one Dirac fermion of mass $|k|$, and
$-i\partial_{y^i}$ acts on the mode as $k_i$, which is its charge exactly as on the circle. For even $n$ the internal chirality matrix
$\gamma_*^K$ anticommutes with $\gamma_K\cdot k$ and exchanges the eigenvalues $+|k|$ and $-|k|$; since the Weyl condition ties the
four-dimensional chirality to $\gamma_*^K$ (@exr-spd-branch-check), each massive Dirac fermion pairs a left-handed spinor of one internal
eigenvector with a right-handed spinor of its image, both with the charges $k_i$. The zero modes are the constant spinors, which
contain both internal chiralities equally (@exm-spd-vanishing-tori).

The square torus is the first case to look at. The first example turns the internal eigenvalues of @exm-spd-torus-two into a
four-dimensional particle spectrum for each of the four spin structures.

::: {#exm-kkf-torus-square}
#### The four spin structures of the square torus

A six-dimensional Dirac fermion on $T^2$ with $R_1 = R_2 = R$ has $N = 2$. With the periodic structure $(P, P)$ there are two massless
Dirac fermions, eight of mass $1/R$ (the lattice points $(\pm1, 0)$, $(0, \pm1)$) and eight of mass $\sqrt2/R$. With $(A, P)$ the lightest
level is $1/(2R)$ with the points $(m_1 + \tfrac12, 0)$, $m_1 \in \{0, -1\}$, hence four Dirac fermions; $(P, A)$ gives the same spectrum
with the roles of the circles exchanged. With $(A, A)$ the lightest level is $1/(\sqrt2R)$ with the four points $(\pm\tfrac12, \pm\tfrac12)$,
hence eight Dirac fermions. The four lattices are drawn in @fig-kkf-torus-lattice.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On the circle a level of mass $n/R$ carried the charges $\pm n/R$. On the torus a level collects every lattice point on a sphere, so
modes of one mass carry different charge vectors, and the second example lists them.

::: {#exm-kkf-torus-charges}
#### Charges at a degenerate level

On the periodic square torus the level $\sqrt5/R$ contains the eight lattice points $(\pm1, \pm2)$ and $(\pm2, \pm1)$, hence sixteen Dirac
fermions with charge vectors $(q_1, q_2)R$ among these eight. The degeneracy is not explained by the $U(1) \times U(1)$ isometry, whose
charges separate the points, but by the discrete symmetries of the square lattice: the reflections $q_i \to -q_i$ and the exchange
$q_1 \leftrightarrow q_2$, a group of order eight that permutes the eight points. A rectangular torus, $R_1 \neq R_2$, keeps only the
reflections, and the level splits into $|(\pm1, \pm2)|$ and $|(\pm2, \pm1)|$ with four points each.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A twist that is not a spin structure breaks even the reflections, because $k \to -k$ maps the twist $\alpha$ to $-\alpha$. The third
example applies twists along two cycles to the gravitino, the Scherk-Schwarz mechanism on the torus.

::: {#exm-kkf-torus-scherk-schwarz}
#### Scherk-Schwarz breaking along two cycles

Let the bosons of a supermultiplet on $T^2$ be periodic and the gravitino twisted by $(\alpha_1, \alpha_2)$, as on the circle in
@exm-kkf-scherk-schwarz. The lightest gravitino has mass $m_{3/2} = \big(\|\alpha_1\|^2/R_1^2 + \|\alpha_2\|^2/R_2^2\big)^{1/2}$, at most
$\tfrac12\big(R_1^{-2} + R_2^{-2}\big)^{1/2}$, reached by the antiperiodic structure $(A, A)$. For $\alpha = (\tfrac14, \tfrac14)$ and $R_1 = R_2 = R$
it is $1/(2\sqrt2R)$ and non-degenerate: the point $(-\tfrac34, \tfrac14)$ already lies higher, at $\sqrt{10}/(4R)$, and $k \to -k$ maps the
twisted lattice to the one with twist $(\tfrac34, \tfrac34)$, a different boundary condition. When the radii differ, a twist along the
large cycle alone, $\alpha = (\tfrac12, 0)$ with $R_1 > R_2$, gives the lower scale $1/(2R_1)$: the breaking scale is set by the
largest twisted cycle.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The six-dimensional torus is the flat internal space of string theory. The fourth example counts the four-dimensional fermions of
a ten-dimensional Weyl spinor on it level by level, and shows that the torus gives no chirality at any level.

::: {#exm-kkf-torus-ten}
#### A ten-dimensional Weyl fermion on $T^6$

For $n = 6$, $N = 8$, and a Weyl spinor in ten dimensions gives $N/2 = 4$ four-dimensional Dirac fermions per lattice point. With the
periodic structure the massless level holds four left-handed and four right-handed Weyl fermions (@exm-spd-torus-six), the level
$1/R$ of a cubic torus twelve lattice points and so $48$ Dirac fermions, and every level is vector-like. With any other spin structure
there are no massless fermions at all. A chiral spectrum from a flat internal space needs a projection, as for the orbifold
$S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$ of @prp-kkf-orbifold-zero-mode or the orbifold $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_3$ of @exm-vcp-orbifold-t6z3, or a gauge background
with flux, as in @exr-spd-torus-flux.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The spectra on rectangular tori are easy to list by machine. The first exercise compares the four spin structures on a torus with
unequal radii, where the two structures with one antiperiodic circle no longer agree.

::: {#exr-kkf-torus-levels}
#### The lightest levels on a rectangular torus

With Sage, list the five lightest four-dimensional mass levels and the number of Dirac fermions at each for a six-dimensional Dirac
fermion on $T^2$ with $R_1 = 1$, $R_2 = \tfrac12$, for the four spin structures. Explain why $(A, P)$ and $(P, A)$ now differ.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @prp-kkf-torus-tower the levels are $|k|^2 = (m_1 + \alpha_1)^2 + 4(m_2 + \alpha_2)^2$, with two Dirac fermions per lattice point:

{{< sage exr-kkf-torus-levels >}}

The antiperiodic condition shifts the momentum of its circle by $1/(2R_i)$: along the large circle $(A, P)$ this costs $\tfrac12$, along the
small one $(P, A)$ it costs $1$. A twist along a large cycle is cheaper, as in @exm-kkf-torus-scherk-schwarz.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The lightest mass with twists is the distance from the origin to the twisted lattice. The second exercise derives the formula of
@prp-kkf-torus-tower and asks when the levels are degenerate in pairs.

::: {#exr-kkf-torus-gap}
#### The gap and the pairing of charges

Show that the lightest mass on $T^n$ with twists $\alpha_i$ is $\big(\sum_i\|\alpha_i\|^2/R_i^2\big)^{1/2}$. Show that the spectrum is invariant
under $k \to -k$, so that every massive level contains the charges $q$ and $-q$ together, if and only if every $\alpha_i \in \{0, \tfrac12\}$,
that is, for a spin structure.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|k|^2 = \sum_i(m_i + \alpha_i)^2/R_i^2$ is a sum of independent terms, each minimised over $m_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ by the integer nearest to
$-\alpha_i$, with minimum $\|\alpha_i\|^2/R_i^2$. The set $\{m + \alpha\}$ is mapped by $k \to -k$ to $\{-m - \alpha\} = \{m' - \alpha\}$, which
equals $\{m + \alpha\}$ iff $2\alpha_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ for every $i$. For other twists the level of $q$ need not contain $-q$, as in
@exm-kkf-torus-scherk-schwarz: the twist breaks charge conjugation of the tower, the conjugate tower being the one with twist $1 - \alpha$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

At high energy the number of four-dimensional fermions is governed by the volume of the torus, as in Weyl's law
(@exr-spd-torus-weyl-law). The third exercise counts them on a three-torus and compares the two extreme spin structures.

::: {#exr-kkf-torus-weyl}
#### Counting the tower on $T^3$

A seven-dimensional Dirac fermion on the cubic torus $T^3$ with $R_i = R$ has $N = 2$. With Sage, count the four-dimensional Dirac fermions of
mass below $E$ for $ER = 2, 5, 10, 20$, with the periodic and the antiperiodic structure, and compare with $N\cdot\tfrac{4\pi}{3}(ER)^3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The count is $N$ times the number of points of $\mathbb{Z}^3 + \alpha$ in the ball of radius $ER$:

{{< sage exr-kkf-torus-weyl >}}

Both ratios tend to $1$: at energies far above $1/R$ the spin structure is invisible and the number of fermions is the volume
$(2\pi R)^3$ of the torus times the density $N(4\pi/3)E^3/(2\pi)^3$ of a seven-dimensional fermion, as for the circle in @exr-kkf-tower-count.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The last statement of the proposition is the reason the torus alone cannot produce the Standard Model. The fourth exercise proves
it for $n = 2$ with explicit matrices and shows that a constant gauge background does not help.

::: {#exr-kkf-torus-chirality}
#### No chirality on $T^2$

On $T^2$ take $\gamma^1_K = \sigma_1$, $\gamma^2_K = \sigma_2$ and $\gamma_*^K = \sigma_3$. Show that $\sigma_3$ maps the eigenvector of $-\sigma\cdot k$
with eigenvalue $|k|$ to the one with eigenvalue $-|k|$, and conclude that at every level the left- and right-handed four-dimensional
spinors are equal in number and charges. Why does a constant gauge potential along $T^2$, a Wilson line, change none of this?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sigma_3$ anticommutes with $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$, so $(-\sigma\cdot k)\sigma_3u = -\sigma_3(-\sigma\cdot k)u = -\lambda\,\sigma_3u$: the eigenvalues
$\pm|k|$ are exchanged. The six-dimensional chirality $\gamma_5 \otimes \sigma_3$ then pairs a left-handed spinor with one internal eigenvector and a
right-handed one with the other, with the same $e^{ik\cdot y}$ and hence the same charges (@prp-kkf-torus-tower). A constant potential
$A = a_idy^i$ only shifts $k$ by $a$, which is a twist (@def-scherk-schwarz-twist, @exr-kkf-wilson-line); the argument holds for every
$k$. Chirality requires a background with flux, $\int_{T^2}F \neq 0$, which no constant potential has (@exr-spd-torus-flux).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

### Exercises

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises of this part combine the tower, the spin structures and the orbifold. Each uses the mode equation of
@prp-kkf-mode-equation together with one of the later statements.

A fermion may carry a charge under a five-dimensional gauge group as well as the Kaluza-Klein charge. The first integrative
exercise computes the tower of such a fermion with Sage.

::: {#exr-kkf-int-charged-tower}
#### Two charges

A five-dimensional fermion of charge $e'$ under a gauge field $B_M$, antiperiodic around the circle, sees a constant $B_y$ with
$e'B_y R = \theta$. With Sage, list for $\theta = 0, \tfrac14, \tfrac12$ the masses below $3/R$ with their multiplicities, find for which $\theta$
a massless fermion exists, and say which degeneracies of the antiperiodic tower the Wilson line lifts.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The internal operator acts on $e^{i(n + \frac12)y/R}$ as $(n + \tfrac12 + \theta)/R$ (@exr-kkf-wilson-line), so the masses are $|n + \tfrac12 +
\theta|/R$, the tower with the total twist $\tfrac12 + \theta$:

{{< sage exr-kkf-int-charged-tower >}}

For $\theta = 0$ every level is doubly degenerate ($n$ and $-n - 1$); for $\theta = \tfrac14$ the degeneracy is lifted completely; for $\theta =
\tfrac12$ the Wilson line cancels the antiperiodicity, a massless mode appears and the levels above it are again paired. A Wilson line
can thus restore a zero mode that the spin structure removed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The zero mode of the orbifold is chiral, and the Pauli term of the circle survives for it. The second integrative exercise
asks what the four-dimensional theory of the zero modes looks like.

::: {#exr-kkf-int-orbifold-pauli}
#### The zero mode on the orbifold

On $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$ the Kaluza-Klein field $A_\mu = g_{\mu y}$ is odd under $y \to -y$ (the metric component $g_{\mu y}$ changes sign), so it has no
zero mode. Using this and @prp-kkf-orbifold-zero-mode, describe the zero modes of a five-dimensional fermion coupled to gravity on
$M^4 \times S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$: chirality, charge, Pauli coupling. Why can a single Weyl fermion not have a Pauli coupling at all?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The zero mode is one Weyl fermion (right-handed for $\eta = 1$). The Kaluza-Klein photon is projected out, so the zero mode has no Kaluza-Klein
charge and nothing to couple to through $F_{\mu\nu}$. Independently of this, $\bar\chi\sigma^{\mu\nu}\chi = \bar\chi_L\sigma^{\mu\nu}\chi_R + \bar\chi_R\sigma^{\mu\nu}
\chi_L$ connects the two chiralities, as a mass does (@exm-kkf-field-strength), so a single Weyl fermion has neither a Dirac mass nor a magnetic
moment: the orbifold removes the magnetic moment of @exm-kkf-zero-mode together with the photon.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Supersymmetry breaking by a twist and by an orbifold can be combined on the same circle. The third integrative exercise
counts the zero modes of a five-dimensional supermultiplet in both cases.

::: {#exr-kkf-int-counting}
#### Zero modes of a hypermultiplet

A five-dimensional hypermultiplet has two complex scalars and one Dirac fermion. Count its massless four-dimensional fields
(complex scalars and Weyl fermions) (a) on the periodic circle, (b) with antiperiodic fermions, (c) on $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$ with
$\psi_R$ even and one of the two scalars even, the other odd. Which case gives a four-dimensional chiral multiplet?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) Two complex scalars and one Dirac fermion, that is two Weyl fermions: two chiral multiplets of opposite chirality, a non-chiral
($\mathcal N = 2$) hypermultiplet. (b) Two complex scalars and no fermion (@exm-kkf-antiperiodic-tower): supersymmetry is broken
(@exm-kkf-scherk-schwarz). (c) One complex scalar and one right-handed Weyl fermion (@prp-kkf-orbifold-zero-mode), which is the
content of one chiral multiplet (equivalently a left-handed one of conjugate charges): the orbifold halves the supersymmetry and
produces chirality: the chiral $N = 1$ multiplets of a hypermultiplet are the even ones, which contain the massless states
[@perezlorenzana2005, Sec. III.C].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

## Exercises {#sec-02-gauge-tower-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The three exercises below combine the two sections of the chapter: the gauge transformation acting on the tower, the
counting of the tower, and the motion of a particle with momentum around the circle. Each of them needs results from both sections.

::: {#exr-kkr-int-charged-scalar}
#### A charged tower in a background field

Take a five-dimensional massless complex scalar on the ansatz with $g = \eta$, $\phi = 1$ and a constant $A_\mu$, with $y \sim y +
2\pi R$. (a) Show with SageManifolds that $\Box_5\Phi = 0$ on $\Phi = f(x)e^{iny/R}$ is $(D_\mu D^\mu + (n/R)^2)f = 0$ with $D_\mu = \partial_\mu -
inA_\mu/R$. (b) Remove $A$ by the reparametrisation $\epsilon = A_\mu x^\mu$ and check that $f$ picks up the phase of
@exm-gauge-charged-modes. (c) What physical effect could a constant $A$ have if one spatial direction of spacetime
were also a circle?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a), (b) For constant $A$ the inverse ansatz is constant and $\Box_5 = \hat g^{AB}\partial_A\partial_B$; the cross terms $-2A^\mu\partial_\mu\partial_y$ and
the term $A^2\partial_y^2$ assemble into $D_\mu D^\mu$ (@exr-kkr-charge-covariant). With $\epsilon = A_\mu x^\mu$, $A' = A - d\epsilon = 0$
and $f' = e^{-in\epsilon/R}f$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-int-charged-scalar >}}

(c) If $x^1 \sim x^1 + 2\pi L$, the parameter $\epsilon = A_1x^1$ is not single valued modulo $2\pi R$ unless $A_1L/R \in \mathbb{Z}$, so a constant $A_1$ cannot be removed: it is the holonomy $\oint A$ of @exr-kkr-shift-horizontal, and it shifts
the momenta of the charged modes along $x^1$ from $k/L$ to $k/L - nA_1/R$, like a twisted boundary condition
(@exr-kkr-charge-twisted). This is the Aharonov-Bohm effect of the Kaluza-Klein photon.
:::

The second exercise counts the tower. It connects the slider of @fig-kk-tower with the density of states of a
five-dimensional field.

::: {#exr-kkr-int-counting}
#### Counting the tower

(a) Show that the number of modes of a five-dimensional massless scalar with mass $m_n < E$ is $N(E) = 2\lfloor ER\rfloor + 1$ for
$ER \notin \mathbb{Z}$. (b) The number of one-particle states with energy below $E$ in a box of volume $V$ is $\sum_n\frac{V}{6\pi^2}(E^2 -
m_n^2)^{3/2}$ for the modes with $m_n < E$. Show that it is $VE^3/6\pi^2$ for $ER < 1$ and approximately $VRE^4/16\pi$ for $ER \gg
1$, the count for a massless field in the five-dimensional volume $V \cdot 2\pi R$. (c) Where is the crossover, and what does a four-dimensional observer conclude from it?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $|n|/R < E$ iff $|n| < ER$, i.e. $n = -\lfloor ER\rfloor, \dots, \lfloor ER\rfloor$, which is the count in the title of the
interactive @fig-kk-tower. (b) For $ER \ll 1$ only $n = 0$ contributes and the count is $\frac{V}{6\pi^2}E^3$, the
four-dimensional density of states. For $ER \gg 1$ the sum over $n$ is approximated by an integral, $\sum_n \approx R\int dp_y$ with
$p_y = n/R$: $\frac{VR}{6\pi^2}\int_{-E}^{E}(E^2 - p^2)^{3/2}dp = \frac{VR}{6\pi^2}\cdot\frac{3\pi}{8}E^4 = \frac{VRE^4}{16\pi}$, which is
$V \cdot 2\pi R$ times the volume $\frac{\pi^2}{2}E^4$ of the four-ball of momenta divided by $(2\pi)^4$: the five-dimensional count. (c) The crossover is at $E
\sim 1/R$: a four-dimensional observer sees the number of states grow faster than $E^3$ above $1/R$ and can infer the
size of the extra dimension from where this happens (@exr-kkr-radius-effective-theory).
:::

The third exercise follows a particle that moves around the circle. It combines the Killing vector, the gauge field
and the masses of the tower.

::: {#exr-kkr-int-particle}
#### A particle with momentum around the circle

A massless particle in five dimensions moves on a geodesic of the ansatz with $\phi = 1$ and $y \sim y + 2\pi R$. (a) Show
that $p_y = \hat g(\partial_y, \dot x)$ is conserved and that quantum mechanics on the circle requires $p_y = -n/R$ (with the sign
convention $\hat g_{yy} = -1$, $p_y = -\dot y - A_\mu\dot x^\mu$). (b) Using @exr-kkr-christoffel-lorentz, show that the
four-dimensional motion is that of a particle of mass $|n|/R$ and charge $n/R$ in the field $F$. (c) Show that the
charge-to-mass ratio is independent of $n$, and compare with @exr-kkr-charge-ratio.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $\partial_y$ is Killing (@def-isometry-u1), so its inner product with the tangent of a geodesic is conserved. The wave
function of the particle around the circle is $e^{iny/R}$ (@prp-kk-periodicity), with momentum $-i\partial_y = n/R$; the
covariant component is $p_y = \hat g_{yy}p^y = -n/R$. (b) The null condition $\hat g(\dot x, \dot x) = 0$ is $g_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot
x^\nu = (\dot y + A\cdot\dot x)^2 = p_y^2$, so with proper time $d\tau = |p_y|\,ds$ the particle is timelike in four dimensions
with $m = |p_y| = |n|/R$ (@exm-kkr-modes-dispersion). With $\dot x = m\,dx/d\tau$ the equation of
@exr-kkr-christoffel-lorentz, $\ddot x^\lambda + \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu = p_yF^\lambda{}_\mu\dot x^\mu$, becomes $m(\frac{d^2x^\lambda}{d\tau^2} +
\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\frac{dx^\mu}{d\tau}\frac{dx^\nu}{d\tau}) = p_yF^\lambda{}_\mu\frac{dx^\mu}{d\tau}$: the Lorentz force on a particle of mass $|n|/R$
and charge of magnitude $|n|/R$, the modes $n$ and $-n$ having opposite charges (the overall sign is the convention
relating $p_y$ to the eigenvalue of $-i\partial_y$). (c) $|q|/m = 1$ in the units of the ansatz, independent of $n$; with the canonical normalisation the charge is $ne$ and
$|q|/m = eR = \sqrt2\kappa$, the result of @exr-kkr-charge-ratio: classical Kaluza-Klein particles, like the quantum modes,
have the extremal charge-to-mass ratio.
:::
